utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is the Celebici appeal, case number IT-96-21-A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Appearances, please. Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours, I'm Upawansa Yapa, appearing for the Prosecution, with Mr. William Fenrick, Mr. Christopher Staker, Mr. Norman Farrell, and Mr. Roeland Bos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: For Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I appear on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my co-counsel from Sarajevo, Edina Residovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is your client here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No he's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of Mr. Mucic are Tom Kuzmanovic and Howard Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, representing Mr. Delic along with Tom Moran from Houston, representing Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Cynthia Sinatra, and along with me is Professor Peter Murphy, representing Esad Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. I propose to ask each of the three appellants who are here whether they can hear the proceedings in a language they understand. Mr. Mucic? THE APPELLANT MUCIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Delic? THE APPELLANT DELALIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And Mr. Landzo? THE APPELLANT LANDZO: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't propose to ask you that each day, but if you have any problem in hearing, please don't hesitate to let us know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have some problems with the French translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you check that, please. Yes, Mr. Yapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the arguments commence, may Your Honours be pleased to give me permission to mention three matters. First is in respect of the request that Your Honour made at the last Status Conference about the confidentiality of any documents, any material in the Prosecution response brief, and we have already informed that there aren't any documents or any material that we wish to have marked confidential or protected in the response brief, and we have indicated that the response brief could be made a public document. The second matter, Your Honours, is we have already handed over an outline of the argument that we propose to present in the course of the proceedings. May I be permitted to hand over copies of the outline. It is only a bare outline, but we feel that it may assist my learned friends and also Your Honours, with great respect, in following the argument we propose to present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This represents only some sort of summary of the material you've already filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: It is. It may be termed a summary of the summary, but we have given the order of argument and made reference to the pages of the brief where the arguments are taken up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: The third matter, Your Honour, is in respect of an oral motion that we intend to make before Your Honours in regard to certain confidential documents which we propose to utilise maybe in the course of the proceedings or in the future. The presentation will be made by Mr. Norman Farrell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, the motion or the documents we've had so far have all been filed on a confidential basis. What is the basis of the need for confidentiality?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. First of all, we've reviewed the documents and the documents don't contain any reference to any confidential witnesses that were made confidential witnesses during the trial, so that certainly isn't a concern. Secondly, one of the reasons is the documents have not been filed with the Court. Obviously, that doesn't preclude their use as public documents, but it was just out of an abundance of caution, in light of the fact there are certain allegations that will made in a tentative form or in the preliminary form in light of the fact that the documents haven't been proved. The authenticity of the signatures haven't been proved. Of course, that will be something if we're successful, and file the documents will be done at trial. So it's the simple fact that there are allegations that will be made as to their relevance, and as the documents have not been filed as matters before this Court, and as they contain allegations which relate to the accused, more out of an abundance of caution for the accused than the Prosecution, we tender them originally as confidential. In terms of their actual content, Your Honour, there's nothing in there that the Prosecution is concerned about per se.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Allegations are made every day in courts. It doesn't mean they've been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's fair enough, but maybe the difference is that we haven't even made a decision, to be frank, yet whether we're proceeding with filing the documents. So until the documents are before you on an actual motion for them being tendered before the Court, that was the only distinction that the Prosecution made, though I accept your position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It's very difficult for us to deal with anything if you haven't made up your mind yet, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, with respect, part of the difficulty in making up our mind, Your Honour, is actually assessing the value and the worth of the documents, and that's the very reason why we bring the motion. Understandably, the previous motion for an adjournment of the oral hearing was denied, particularly on the basis that there wasn't a determination of whether the documents had any relevance to the issues before the appellant Chamber. As a result, with this oral motion we've filed with the Court, as you're aware, Your Honour, and with the Defence counsel, the documents, five documents in translation, which I'm intending to, with the Court's indulgence, to make submissions on the relevance of these documents, simply for the purpose of requesting that the proceedings not be closed at the end of the oral hearing, at the end of this week, and that if the Court grants it, that the Court permit, within a reasonable period of time, the filing of written submissions on the documents solely for the purpose of determining their admissibility under Rule 115. And if they are admissible under Rule 115 and they could have affected the verdict, that they then are considered by the Court for the purposes of remitting the matter back to the Trial Chamber. Essentially the standard application for fresh evidence, or new additional evidence under Rule 115, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, is the only basis upon which you're addressing us, upon which you're addressing us at the moment, is that you want the matter kept open; you're not going to argue that they should be admitted as fresh evidence or that they should be taken into account, but you want to be able to argue at some subsequent stage that we should take them into account on one basis or the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's basically the summary of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is, of course, a third situation you may like to consider: that they be relevant, if they are relevant, only to a reconsideration of the evidence rather than as a fresh evidence point. If a matter is being reheard, as it were, in the Appeals Chamber, as I understand it, it would be heard upon the current state of the material available.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Maybe I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you fail to get them in as fresh evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- and nevertheless persuade us that we should reconsider this issue of command responsibility about Mr. Delalic, then we would have to reconsider it on the material which is presently available, would we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. The purpose of the argument this week is to demonstrate the errors of law or errors of fact, and that this is a subsequent argument. And in fact, if we are correct, if we do file them and if they do meet the Rule 115 standard, the approach would be that if it could affect the verdict or demonstrate under Tadic that the verdict was unsafe, then presumably the appropriate remedy would be that a new trial should be ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's something which we can consider at a later stage, but at this stage there is nothing wrong with us proceeding with the Prosecution appeal in relation to Mr. Delalic. And all you want us to do is to decide to leave your options open; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That would be fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, what would you like to say in relation to that very narrow issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. As I've indicated, there are five documents, Your Honour, that were placed before you, and I understand they've been given to Defence counsel as well. They include both the original version, which is the Serbo-Croat version, and a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We don't have the original. We only have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry. Just one moment, Your Honour. My apologies. If I could seek the assistance of the usher. Thank you, sir. These are the complete versions of both, Your Honour. The reference to the documents obviously has to at least meet some type of minimum threshold, the threshold being that they are of significant relevance, or potential relevance, in fact, to the matters before you, that they relate to the issues regarding the culpability of the appellants such as there is a basis for granting the adjournment. So I will take the steps of going through them very briefly just to indicate the relevance or the potential relevance. The first document which is before you, document number 37 -- I should indicate that the document number, Your Honours, doesn't indicate -- isn't specifically defined in relation to those matters that have been indexed or translated. This is a number the Prosecution gave to the documents when they arrived in the office. Document 37 is July 18th, 1992. You'll see from the original that it's a draft order, with apparently handwritten corrections on it. At the end of the draft order it's signed by apparently Mr. Delalic, with the name written in as to Commander TG-1. If you look at the document itself, it's dated July 18th, 1992, and the document indicates in the first sentence that it's on the basis of the appointment made by the Main Staff of the Bosnian armed forces, then it gives the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down when reading, for the benefit of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's not the first time that it's been said to you, Mr. Farrell, so please keep it in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm fond that you remembered. If I can begin by reviewing the document again. It's dated July 18th, 1992. The document reads, in the first sentence: "On the basis of the appointment made by Main Staff BH armed forces, number 02/349-343, from 11 July 1992, and the order with the force of law of BH armed forces." And then the next line states, in capital letters: "I hereby appoint ..." And then it states, "For the duties in TG-1 Konjic the following persons." And I'd simply ask you to note, Your Honours, that the first one is an individual by the name of Ceravac. If you turn to the second part of the translation, you'll see that about two thirds of the way down, it says -- just more than half down, I'm sorry, "Assistant to commander for moral education Smajo Prevljak." And then three places below that, the appointment of the supervisor of the regional prison in Celebici, Zdravko Mucic. In the Prosecution's submissions, the potential relevance, assuming that the document is accepted, is first of all the date of the letter is July 18th, 1992; and the letter, apparently signed by Mr. Delalic, demonstrates his knowledge of an order on July 11, 1992. The position of the Defence at trial was that the accused at trial, Mr. Delalic, had no knowledge of the order until sometime after July 27, as he was carrying out operations on Mount Igman, and that he didn't actually take over any responsibility until July 30th in relation to the -- his role in all the formations. And this was found by the Trial Judge. This document, if accepted, potentially demonstrates that in fact that's not the case, that Mr. Delalic clearly took over as commander prior to July 30th, that he is aware of his appointment, at least on July 18th, and that as a result he takes actions regarding the appointment. The second demonstrable relevance is that in the judgement and the position of the Defence of Delalic at trial, as quoted in the judgement at paragraph 674, is that Mr. Delalic had no knowledge as to when and how Mr. Mucic became a warden of the prison. Well, with respect to that position at trial, it appears it's directly contradicted by this document in that if this document is accepted, it appears, on the face of the document, that Mr. Delalic is actually appointing Mr. Mucic as the regional prison commander of Celebici, and, importantly, it's for duties in Tactical Group 1 in Konjic. So not only is he appointing Mr. Music; it appears, from the face of it, that there is some evidence from which to conclude that these are duties within the command of Tactical Group 1, something that the Defence has alleged and the Trial Chamber has found, that there was no relation between Tactical Group 1 and the prison. Thirdly, I would note that there appears -- once again this is all on the face of the document, and I appreciate that the Defence may, if they are filed, refute them, but on the face of the document it says that for the duties of Tactical Group 1 there's an appointment of -- excuse my pronunciation -- Mr. Ceravac, which is number one, assistant to the head of staff for operative educational work. You'll recall that in July of 1992, Mr. Delalic signed some documents -- these are release documents -- and that the Trial Chamber concluded that he was signing these release documents on behalf of Mr. Ceravac and that Mr. Cerovac testified that though he didn't have any direct control over the prison, he had asked Mr. Delalic to sign on his behalf. I would submit that this is clearly called into question by the fact that in fact Mr. Ceravac is his subordinate. He's not signing it on behalf of Mr. Ceravac. The inference may be drawn from the evidence that in fact Mr. Ceravac couldn't do it and, as the superior to Mr. Ceravac in Tactical Group 1, he took over the position. These are just inferences on the face of the document, I understand. The last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have you got a paragraph reference to the judgement there?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: For Mr. Ceravac? No, I'm sorry, I will have to get it for you. If you don't mind, I'll continue until I can. I'll try and find that as I'm going along, Your Honour. The last point to be made with respect to the first document is that you will recall that the release orders that were signed by Mr. Delalic, there were three of them in July, and the first one was on July 17th. The second one, as I recall, for Dr. Grubac, was the 22nd of July, and the third one for Witness P, you'll recall, was on the 22nd of July as well. The Trial Chamber finds that Mr. Delalic was, in fact, a coordinator during this time because he didn't take over the position as Tactical Group 1 commander until after July 27th, presumably the 30th of July. That being the case, they accept that he was signing for the head of investigations for these release orders and, therefore, had no authority himself. If you look at this draft order, it's dated July the 18th. This is around the same time as the first release order was signed and certainly prior to the signing of the two release orders on July 22nd. If this document is accepted, Mr. Delalic was not the coordinator during this time, and he was not a civilian coordinator who had no authority, and he was not simply signing on someone else's behalf, although I think it was the head of the investigations. The inference can be drawn from this that on July 22nd when Dr. Grubac and Witness P were released, their release orders were signed by Mr. Delalic as his -- in his capacity as commander and as the commander, he has a supervisory role over the Celebici prison. That being the case, the release orders were not signed as a coordinator on behalf of someone else that indicate no evidence of command responsibility. Those are the references I wanted to make to the first document. In relation to your question about the relation to Mr. Ceravac, I'm just going to attempt to -- it appears to be at paragraph 685.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The second document Your Honours, is the one numbered 120, dated the 30th of October, 1992. This is apparently, a document from Smajo Prevljak, who is the deputy commander for morale. It's from October the 30th, 1992, and if the previous document is accepted, you'll be able to draw the inference, the trier of fact will, I'm sorry, that Mr. Prevljak, in fact was subordinate to Mr. Delalic under the appointment for the duties of Tactical Group 1 Konjic. The letter is to the Konjic War Presidency, and it's with regard to the act of the commander of Tactical Group 1 from a particular date, and it's a report to the War Presidency. The commander of Tactical Group 1, it's clearly submitted, is Mr. Delalic in October of 1992 as found by the Trial Chamber. The singular importance of this document is found, in the Prosecution's submission, at the top of the second page of the translation. The document is with respect to the military investigation commission. This is the commission that was to look into the prisoners detained at Celebici prison for their classification and potential release. At the top of page 2 of the document, it says the investigation of the imprisoned persons in the prison of Celebici was conducted by an investigation commission that was composed of experts which was formed by Mr. Delalic, and the inference to be drawn is, therefore, he did have control, at least in the formation of this commission. You will recall in the evidence, as found by the Trial Chamber, that at one point in time Mr. Delalic -- I think it was on June the 2nd -- was at a meeting in the administration building of the Celebici prison camp, and this is at paragraph 678 of the judgement. The witness was Witness D, and he indicated that Mr. Delalic and most members of the military investigative commission met on the 1st of June, 1992 at the Celebici prison camp. Mr. Delalic, according to the witness and as is stated by the Trial Chamber, "Appeared to be directing the proceedings. He read out some kind of order which had arrived by fax, which Mr. Delalic explained to them as indicating how they were to conduct the interrogation of detainees based on a list of categories." The Trial Chamber recognises this fact and that the categories of detainees were read out from the facts. This is in paragraph 681. The Trial Chamber then is cautious to attribute the creation of the categories, this is the categories of prisoners who are to be released, to Mr. Delalic. And they further find that there was no evidence that Mr. Delalic had any position of authority or superiority over any of the members in the investigative commission and that Mr. Delalic could not exercise any authority over the prison camp at Celebici, its commanders or its personnel. This is at paragraph 682. It appears, from the face of this document, that at a minimum, he had some authority over the investigation commission to the extent that, in fact, the investigation commission into the prison itself was formed by Mr. Delalic. I'll now refer to the third document, number 137. This is a document which is dated the 14th of November, 1992. You will recall that the evidence appears to be that by mid-November, sometime around November 17th or thereafter, Mr. Delalic is no longer acting as commander of TG-1. It's not clear, but it's in the mid of November. There was, of course, the document which was excluded, which had some -- I'll deal with it when I come to the documents that are excluded on the face of the matter before the Trial Chamber. This is a letter to Mr. Delalic as the commander of TG-1. It's from the chief of the prison guards in the Musala prison. The Musala prison, as you're aware, is not the Celebici prison. It's a sports hall where -- essentially the sports hall where people were detained, as I understand it. This is a complaint made directly to Mr. Delalic, as the commander of Tactical Group 1, with respect to Mr. Hazim Delic. It seems a little odd that if there was no relationship between the two, that the platoon commander and chief of prison guards in one prison is complaining about the conduct of Mr. Delic directly to a tactical group commander who allegedly has no control authority and involvement whatsoever in relation to people who work in the prison. The complaint is not directly with respect to the Celebici prison camp but with respect to the acts, in other words, the conduct of Mr. Delic. And the complaint is apparently, on the face of this document, to his commander in relation to his conduct. Therefore, the inference, it is submitted, can be easily drawn that he thought that Mr. Delic is the subordinate. Why else would another commander be submitting a report on the conduct of someone who has no relationship and is not a subordinate? The document submitted indicates that Delalic did have authority over Mr. Delic. It also, it is submitted, indicates that Mr. Delic is, therefore, part of Tactical Group 1, which is consistent with the first document that I referred to which showed that the Celebici prison fell under the duties of Tactical Group 1. I would note that on the first page of translation, at the end of the page, the last full paragraph starts with the words, "He was also regularly boasting". That "he" is Mr. Delic, and he is boasting to the prisoners, it appears in the Musala, when he entered the Musala prison, and it states that he, that is Mr. Delic -- I'm sorry, Mr. Delic I'm talking about: "Mr. Delic was also regularly boasting to the prisoners that he," Mr. Delic, "could release any prisoner he wanted while I," that's the commander of -- the chief of prison staff, "was not able to do that because he said he had the stamp of TG-1. Thus he released from the Celebici prison the prisoner Ratko Vujicic who had been his colleague at work. MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, will take him to the prison again today." it's submitted that the reference here is that TG-1 obviously has authority over the prison if Mr. Delic is using its stamp to personally remove people from the prison who are his former colleagues. On the second page, in relation to a comment by the chief of the prison guards about the visit of the International Committee of the Red Cross, he indicates that there was a complaint that he, the author of this document, did not allow members of the International Committee of the Red Cross to visit. What he states in the letter essentially is that they could visit but he was hesitant to actually allow him to interview the detainees without witness, which is a condition of ICRC visits to prisoners of war. The explanation for that, not permitting them to interview without witness, is given and it states that he was requesting the clearance of the supervisor of the prison, Mr. Mucic, or another person of Tactical Group 1. It appears he's seeking clearance from people who are his superiors which go up the chain to Tactical Group 1. Lastly, he, in the second last paragraph, the last line and the last paragraph, he asks Mr. Delalic, as the commander of Tactical Group 1, to prohibit Mr. Delic's entrance to the premises of Musala prison and also asks Mr. Delalic, in the very last sentence, to review the list of released prisoners as well as the whole work of the administration of Celebici prison. Once again, it seems a little odd, in light of the Trial Chamber's judgement, that a member of another prison, who is the Chief of Staff and who is involved in the detention of prisoners in the region at the time, is indicating that a tactical group commander, who allegedly has nothing to do with the prison, actually take control over one of the subordinates of the prison, give orders as to who can enter the prison, grant clearance as to whether an international organisation can speak with detainees, prohibit Mr. Delic from entering the prison by his own order, and to review the release -- list of released prisoners and the administration of Celebici prison. The next document is document 62. This is dated August 21, 1992. It's signed by Pavo, so the inference that would have to be drawn is that Pavo is the -- is Mr. Mucic and the commander of the prison. The first sentence states: "In respect of the detention of Petko Grubac in the Celebici barracks, the director of the barracks declares the following." It's submitted that the inference is that Mr. Mucic, Pavo, is writing a report with respect to the detention and subsequent release of a detainee at Celebici prison. This detainee is Dr. Grubac, which we know his testimony is referred to by the Trial Chamber and he's one of the persons who a release order, as I recall, on July 22nd, is signed by Mr. Delalic. The significance, it is submitted, is that the report -- there's a report and an order. The order doesn't relate to the prison, it relates to persons who appear to have occupied Mr. Grubac's apartment, but the significance, from the Prosecution's perspective, is the report itself on the release and -- the detention and subsequent release of a detainee is sent to commander of Tactical Group 1. If you look at the copies to be -- on the second page of the translation, Your Honours, it says, "To be delivered to supervisor of the prison," presumably this is Mucic copying himself, the commander of Tactical Group 1, the person detained himself; and the municipal secretariat. It's important to note that the only military body and the only body of authority addressed here is to Tactical Group 1. It's not addressed to the Konjic Territorial Defences or the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, the police. And clearly, in the Prosecution's submission, there is an inference that could be drawn, if this document is accepted, consistent with the others that the reporting mechanism and the command structure goes to Tactical Group 1. The last document which I refer to and which is before you is that dated August the 7th, 1992. This is not in direct relation to the prison itself but what it demonstrates is, in the Prosecution's submission, the link between Tactical Group 1 and the Konjic municipal staff of the Bosnian armed forces. This is a warming, in relation to a previous order, to the Konjic municipal staff of the armed forces from Mr. Delalic. Now, the Trial Chamber, as we know, distinguished between the role of Tactical Group 1 from the activities of the territorial forces or armed forces in Konjic. This appears to be on its face an order by Mr. Delalic to the municipal staff of the armed forces in Konjic, and, therefore, he is subordinating them to himself as commander of Tactical Group 1, and this goes to the role he plays in the region consistent with, it is submitted, the first document. Your Honours, I apologise for taking a little bit of your time, but this is the submitted potential relevance of the documents and the basis upon which the Prosecution seeks the -- at least the opportunity to fully review the documents. If the Prosecution, after reviewing all the documents, is of the view that it would have rendered, at least in the Prosecution's submission, the conviction unsafe, which appears to be the requirement under Rule 115 of the Tadic decision, then the remedy requested is that the proceedings not be closed, that there be a time period for the filing of this, that if the Prosecution does not intend to file a Rule 115 application, that it simply file a notice with the Court indicating such and at that point in time, if it does not, the proceedings will be closed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is your application restricted to these five documents or is somebody beavering his way through the documents to see if there's anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, I hope they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So there may be other documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: These are simply a sample to try and address your concerns that there was nothing of relevance put before you on the previous motion, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. Well, Mr. Ackerman, we certainly don't expect you to answer the point made about the relevance unless you can demonstrate that everything the Prosecution has said is wrong. All I think we need to determine at this stage is whether we permit the Prosecution to keep its options open. What would you like to say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with regard to that specific question, the Rules permit the Prosecutor to keep their options open. We're in a kind of a procedural limbo here because if they wanted to bring new material to the attention of the Appeals Chamber, the Rules say that should have happened at least 15 days prior to the date set for hearing the appeal. The other option that the Prosecution and the Defence have is that within one year after the judgement on this appeal to apply for a review. So it seems one of those two options is what is open to the Prosecutor or any of us with regard to this matter. I have just seen these documents for the first time this morning just as you have, so I'm not in any kind of position to deal with them at all. We might want, later on in this proceeding, to make a very short submission similar to what the Prosecution has made. It's very clear that if these documents are going to be considered at any stage of these proceedings, a great deal more than just submission of the documents is required because there's serious question, at least in my mind, regarding their authenticity, who authored them. One of them has no signature at all. So there's a great deal of additional information that would be necessary before their content and their alleged import could be considered by this Chamber or any other Chamber. What I would prefer to do at this point, Your Honour, is leave the matter as it stands, with the possibility that we would request some time later on in these proceedings for just a few moments to address the Chamber regarding these matters before we depart for other places. But I think it seems to me that the proper way to proceed at this point is to -- for the Prosecutor to simply go on with their business regarding these documents, and if after the judgement has been entered on this appeal they determine that there's a basis for an application for review based on these documents, then let them file that. It's clear that whatever's done with these documents, it's going to require the taking of evidence from witnesses regarding their authenticity, whether or not they were actually delivered, signed, things of that nature. One of them has no signature, I've noticed. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, if we deferred any decision on it, it would mean after the end of the argument by the Prosecution on the command responsibility issues, they would simply say, "We leave our case open." It's at that stage I see the issue arising. If you have no objection to them doing that so that you have the opportunity, perhaps tomorrow or the next day, to address us on keeping it open throughout and you have no objection to them not closing their argument at this stage, then we need not decide it at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not absolutely certain about my position at this point, but I think my position is this, Your Honour: That having not made the application 15 days before the date set for oral argument, that the Prosecution's remedy at this point is post-judgement application for review, so that we should simply close the matter at this point, the arguments be heard, that the Chamber make its ruling, whatever that is, file its judgement, announce its judgement, and then if the Prosecution, within one year after that, determines that there are documents that justify review, then bring it up in the review procedures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not altogether certain that you are correct on that. This would be a review, I would have thought, of the Trial Chamber's decision rather than of our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The Rule indicated it can be either of a Trial Chamber or an Appeals Chamber decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we won't argue it now, but there may be a problem from the Prosecution's point of view. Well, then, you're objecting that if at the end of the argument today they say, "We want to leave it open," you object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You had said that you wanted some time to make some further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's what we would like to do. As I stand here right now, I would object to that, but we have just seen these. I haven't had a chance to consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand, and so have we just seen them perhaps a quarter of an hour before you did, but at the end of the Prosecution argument the issue arises. Are they entitled to say at that stage, "We still want you to consider allowing these documents in but we don't press for a decision on that at this stage." Now, if you object to that at that stage, we're going to have to say whether we permit them to keep their options open at least until sometime towards the end of the hearing or shortly after it. I understand what you say about the 15-day rule. That's something that can be extended and the Rules permit that if explained. I'm not suggesting one way or the other which way the Appeals Chamber would decide it, but they asked for an adjournment, and that was refused on the basis that we thought they could proceed with their appeal. Now, if you still object at the close of their argument, we will have to decide at that stage whether we permit them to keep their options open; not to admit the documents, but just to keep their options open. If you want extra time to consider that particular application, to keep their options open, for myself, I'd be happy to give it to you. But we still have to make a decision one way or the other, even if to defer the decision at the end of the Prosecution's argument on these grounds of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, and what I would like to do is state my position on that at some later stage, probably today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm hoping that the Prosecution will have finished their argument on command responsibility, surely before the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would think so. I would suspect there would be a break at some point. I just need to consult with Ms. Residovic a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's perfectly reasonable, as long as you understand that we have to make a decision one way or the other at the conclusion of the Prosecution case on these grounds of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add something. I would like to say something to Mr. Ackerman. If I understand rightly, you say that since the time allowed had not been respected, the 15 days, then the Prosecutor would have to ask for a review of the judgement because of new facts being presented. The problem is that in the situation we have here, these facts come up after the judgement has been given, whereas here we are at the beginning of the hearing for oral applications. We are not here talking about the review of a judgement that has been given, a judgement that is definite, and where you have new facts arising after the judgement, because the new facts we have now have arisen before the judgement has been given. So I would like you to have this in mind when you speak later on. I'm not asking you to speak about that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ackerman, clearly there will be a break during the course of the argument on the Prosecution's treatment of the command responsibility grounds. I think we are entitled to ask you at the end of that break what attitude you're going to take to keeping their options open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I will tell you at that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, now, Mr. Yapa, who is dealing with the command responsibility? I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If it please Your Honour, you will see from those documents that they are also pertinent to the case of Pavo Mucic. Now, I appreciate that the position of Mucic is very different from the others in this case, but those documents cause us very considerable concern at this stage in the proceedings, and it's pertinent to the matters just raised a moment ago by your honourable and learned colleague. My learned friend, Mr. Kuzmanovic has tried unsuccessfully to obtain documents from Croatia before now, and on the face of it some of the documents which the Prosecution have are exactly the sort of documents we would like to have seen, not only for the appellate purposes, but they would have been very useful at trial. They're fundamental as far as Mr. Mucic is concerned. They go not only to the basis of his conviction but to the scope of his conviction, because he was only convicted upon the basis of superior command responsibility in respect of his command of or supervision of the Celebici prison. These documents are exactly germane to that. And the knock-on effect in this case is enormous, because it goes to other issues, other findings contained in the judgement, not least the question of sentence. For myself and for my learned friend Mr. Kuzmanovic, we're very grateful for the Prosecution for providing the samples of documents which they have. We've seen five, three of which are extremely germane, and we are very keen to explore the possibility of their use, not simply as an adjunct to this appeal, but as part of the body of the appeal itself. There are 149 other documents. We have no idea at the moment what they may be. But if they are of such moment to Mr. Mucic's case as three of these five documents are, then the position of Mr. Mucic on appeal may be fundamentally altered in two ways: first in respect of what he himself can advance through counsel, or potentially by the calling of witnesses that we simply did not know existed until the production of these documents. The other thing it may do is alter the Prosecution's own position as to Mr. Mucic, because they've been advancing, for instance, certain dates as to his supervision of the prison, and they may take a different view of that when all the documents are at hand. So it may be that concessions will come from the Prosecution side, and I appreciate they can't even begin to consider that matter until they have seen, correlated, and analysed all of those documents. But let me suppose for the moment that as far as providence, accuracy, and relevance of the documents are concerned, that the Appeal Chamber is satisfied to the extent that they become admissible in these proceedings in some form or another. What is the effect? Are we really going to have an appeal judgement based upon the facts of a trial which may be easily proved to be erroneous, upon a judgement which may have been reached upon the basis of a lack of information or of false information? It seems to me that in those circumstances the potential for a miscarriage of justice is vast. Now, we didn't see these documents until this morning and we had no input into the Prosecution's application for an adjournment of certain parts of this appeal until those documents have been analysed and placed before the Court. But for Mr. Mucic, Mr. Kuzmanovic and I are extremely concerned that there should be any further consideration of Mr. Mucic's appeal as to command responsibility and as to the knock-on effect of that, whatever it may be, until we've had sight of all of those documents and we're able to put the matters before the Court in a proper and coherent way. As your learned colleague said, this isn't a question of information coming to an appellant court post-judgement; this is information which has come to this Court pre-judgement, and it seems to me to ignore it is to make ourselves hostages to very dangerous fortune.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is the basis of your remarks the prospect that you too may be making an application for these documents to be admitted as fresh evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: It's quite possible. Certainly in respect of three of those documents, we would dearly have loved to have had them in our possession. I wasn't involved in the trial. I didn't come into this case until appellate proceedings were virtually -- well, I came in just before sentencing. But it would have made a very considerable difference to the way that Mr. Mucic's appeal had been conducted had, for instance, these documents surfaced a week after the judgement. There would have been a very different approach, I think both by the Prosecution and by Mr. Mucic. Now, I accept that I'm treading on toes in all sorts of ways, and the last thing I want to do is be the cause of adjournments and delays. But if I don't raise this matter now, I'm doing no service to my client. There is in this case a very real potential for a very real miscarriage of justice, and now is the time, with respect, to address it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest that during the adjournment -- there is obviously a great deal of material which we can go on with, but during the adjournment you speak to the Prosecution, hopefully the Prosecution will break its usual rule and talk to counsel for the Defence, and find out what the timetable is likely to be for them to have all the documents translated so that you know what position you're going to be in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Making a submission of this nature before an appellate court 18 or 19 months after the judgement is as attractive as rolling naked downhill in a barrel of fish hooks, as somebody once said to me, but it has to be made, and whatever the consequences. I think, by and large, my relations with the Prosecution are good enough for them to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, may I suggest you do talk to them so that we're in a better position to know just where we're heading. And we can nevertheless go on with the appeal at this stage, bearing in mind that you foreshadowing an application for an adjournment of anything dealing with your client's command responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I'm much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Yapa. Who is dealing with this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, the argument to be taken up will be in respect of grounds of appeal falling within group 1. The first matter is in respect of command responsibility. That is ground 1 of the Prosecution's grounds of appeal. It will be dealt with by Mr. William Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Fenrick.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I would intend to do here over the course of approximately one half hour is give you an overview of the Prosecution's approach to the law of command responsibility so that we would try and address a range of legal issues and at the same time provide you with a complete picture of the doctrine itself, as this is perhaps the first time when this Chamber has addressed this range, the whole spectrum of command responsibility issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you for a moment, Mr. Fenrick. In your submissions you refer to the World War II cases. I know that we do have the Nuremberg judgments in the library here, but I don't think we've got all of the Japanese ones. If you're going to rely upon any of these, we really do need copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would be referring very briefly -- well, first of all, I don't expect to be making a large number of case references, to be quite honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you've referred to them generally in your submissions, and if you want us to look at this sort of thing, I'm afraid we're going to have to ask you to provide copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It's our understanding everything is in the book of authorities, Your Honour. Now, if I may start, first of all it's the position of the Prosecution that Article 7(3) of our Statute is not all by itself some kind of a code. What it does is incorporate the existing law relating to the doctrine of command responsibility. Secondly, the existing law, or the entire doctrine of command responsibility is basically rooted in custom or case law. If one looks, for example, at the statute for the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg, or the statute which applied to the Tokyo trials, or Control Counsel Law number 10, which regulated a lot of the subsequent proceedings at Nuremberg, in no case is there any reference to a doctrine of command responsibility. When those statutory or treaty provisions refer to criminal liability, essentially what they are concerned with is the traditional doctrine of individual criminal responsibility, referring to perpetrators and people who order, incite, or aid and abet. The doctrine of command responsibility, it is our submission, originated essentially in an application of what might be referred to as a doctrine of aiding and abetting for superiors to the kinds of situations which we had in the post World War II period. And I think, or I submit, that we've got to place a very considerable emphasis on those post World War II decisions and bear in mind what they are. They aren't rooted in a treaty provision, or at least not rooted to a great extent. Beyond the post World War II cases, what we have is Additional Protocol I, which applies to international conflicts, and there are two articles in that Additional Protocol I: Articles 86 and 87. Those two, although they have been referred to by some as codifying the doctrine of command responsibility, we would submit are at best a partial codification of the doctrine. To a considerable extent, even to interpret Articles 86 and 87, we have to pay considerable emphasis to what the customary law is outside of those articles, or outside of Additional Protocol I. It's the submission of the Prosecution, which we would suggest is essentially uncontested, that there are three essential elements for command responsibility for failure to act. The first of these essential elements is the existence of some form of superior subordinate relationship. This particular element, or the interpretation of this element, is particularly relevant to this case in two respects. One -- and what I will be doing later is talking about each of these elements in turn. But just to highlight things, in connection with the superior subordinate relationship, there is a question of whether or not that relationship applies to instances of what might be called influence -- that's particularly relevant with reference to the Delalic appeal -- and also with whether or not the superior subordinate relationship applies to de facto in addition to de jure relationships is relevant to the appeal of Mr. Mucic. The second element is that the superior new or had reason to know that a criminal act was about to be or had been committed. The interpretation of this particular provision is, we submit, an important point of law, which we have requested the Court to rule on, specifically, what the meaning of "had reason to know" is, but it is not directly relevant to the appeals of any of the individual accused in this case. The third element is that the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal act or punish the perpetrator thereof. It is our understanding that the meaning of that particular provision is not in issue here, but we shall nevertheless refer to it very briefly. Now, if I may discuss the superior subordinate relationship, the first essential element that we have submitted exists, or must exist for a command responsibility case. Normally, in most cases, when the doctrine of command responsibility applies, there is some kind of a hierarchical relationship, a chain of command, between the perpetrators or the units to which the perpetrators belong and the person in command or the person holding a position of superior authority. It is, however, the submission of the Prosecution that this doctrine can also apply to a wider range of categories of superiors. It is our submission that the relationship exists when a superior has effective control over the persons committing the underlying violations, in the sense of having some kind of material ability to prevent and punish. It is also certainly our submission that the doctrine of command responsibility can apply to both civilian and military leaders. The duty to prevent or punish arises from the power to control perpetrators in a particular set of circumstances as well as in certain general circumstances. In particular, it's our submission that a direct relationship of superior and subordinate, that is, a direct chain of command between the perpetrator and the superior, is not necessary. The superior may have responsibility for an area in which the perpetrator commits an offence. For example, in the High Command in the Hostages cases, both of which are referred to in the Trial Chamber judgement, the military commanders were held responsible in some cases because they had some kind of an area or zone of occupation responsibility, and they were held responsible even if they did not have direct command responsibility over the units which were in the area and which had committed offences. Somewhat similarly, the superior may exercise a substantial degree of influence over the perpetrator or over the entity to which the perpetrator belongs. And with reference, as substantiation for those propositions, we refer to the Muto case, which is referred to in the Trial Chamber judgement, and also Hirota and Roechling. These cases are discussed at paragraphs 355 to 363 in the Trial Chamber judgement. Those cases involved people in a range of different circumstances. Muto was a Japanese general who was the chief of staff for General Yamashita, and it was held that although Muto, or General Muto, was not in a chain of command, he had, because of his position as chief of staff, a substantial degree of influence over what was happening in the units which were subordinate to the headquarters to which he was chief of staff. Hirota, of course, was a Japanese foreign minister, who clearly had no direct ability to -- certainly did not have the soldiers who were committing offences subordinate to him in some kind of a chain of command. And Roechling involved German industrialists, who once again did not have a strict hierarchical relationship between the perpetrators and the individuals committing the offence. If I might also refer to Article 87 of Additional Protocol I, which talks about the duty of military commanders, it says: "The high contracting parties and parties to the conflict shall require military commanders with respect to members of the armed forces under their command and other persons under their control to prevent and, where necessary, suppress breaches." Clearly, even the Additional Protocols envisage something more than a strictly hierarchical relationship for the imposition of command responsibility. As indicated in the Prosecution's appeal, in our brief, paragraphs 3.22 and 3.27 to 3.53, the Prosecution submits that the doctrine of superior responsibility includes liability for a person who, although not a superior in a direct chain of command over the perpetrator, exercises sufficient control, authority, or power of substantial influence, that is, to have the material ability to prevent or punish the commission of the crimes. The Prosecution certainly does not suggest or submit in any way that Article 7(3) includes any person who exercises some influence in a given situation. For example, one could easily envisage a situation where a journalist has some knowledge of an offence that either is about to be committed or has been committed, and technically, by publicising that fact, he or she may have some impact on whether or not the offence is committed or whether there is punishment for it. But certainly a journalist, although a person of influence, would not be someone who would be scooped into this substantial influence aspect of command responsibility, which we submit exists. If we might give another example of where we would not think the doctrine would apply, it would not apply to, say, military commanders when you have two formations side by side, one in one area, one in another, and the commander of one formation becomes aware of, for whatever reasons, or doesn't become aware of, offences being committed by a similar level formation next door. We would certainly not submit that the side-by-side commander is one who would be scooped up within this doctrine of command responsibility. But we would submit that if there is this substantial influence, which we concede is something which has got to be determined essentially on a case-by-case basis, if this superior does have the material ability to prevent or punish, he or she should be within the confines of this doctrine of command responsibility as set forth in Article 7(3). And as a last observation in connection with the superior subordinate relationship aspect, clearly, on the basis of our case law, including, one might add, the Aleksovski appeal position, a superior may be held liable because he or she possesses de jure or de facto authority or a combination of both. There is no requirement that the authority be de jure exclusively. In fact, if one just relied on de jure responsibility, one could end up with ludicrous results. I believe that the Queen of England, for example, would technically be listed as the commander-in-chief of the British Armed Forces, but one would not suggest that the Queen is someone who should be held liable on the basis of the doctrine of command responsibility. One must look at de facto responsibility in addition to a technical de jure qualification. What is significant is not the title that a person holds, whether they be called a commander, a deputy commander, or a coordinator, or any range of labels. What is significant is the actual reality of their superior authority. That is all I have to say, Your Honours, in connection with the superior subordinate relationship aspect. I would now propose to move on to the "knew or had reason to know" issue, unless there were any questions. In that case, I will move on to "knew or had reason to know." There is certainly no question, one would submit, that someone could be held liable on the basis of 7(3) if proof of actual knowledge had been established, and that, of course, can be established by either direct or circumstantial evidence. The real issue is what is the meaning of "had reason to know." Does it mean that one must prove that there is information virtually in the hands of the superior or does it mean something a little bit broader? It is the submission of the Prosecution that "had reason to know" refers to situations where either the superior has information which puts him or her on notice or which tends to suggest that subordinates were about to commit or had committed crimes. That essentially is the approach that was adopted by the Trial Chamber, if I recollect accurately. And in addition, however, it is the submission of the Prosecution that "had reason to know" also includes the situation where a superior had no such information in his or her actual possession, but lacked such information as a result of a serious dereliction of his or her duty to obtain information of a general nature within his or her reasonable access relating to the conduct of his or her subordinates. If I might draw the attention of Your Honours to the Blaskic decision in addition to the Celebici decision. In the Blaskic trial decision, in fact the Trial Chamber came to a conclusion about the meaning of "had reason to know" which is essentially similar to this somewhat broader approach taken by the Prosecution vis-a-vis the Trial Chamber in the Celebici case. If I may just quote very briefly. In Blaskic, paragraph 332, the Trial Chamber found that: "If a commander has exercised due diligence in the fulfillment of his duties, yet lacks knowledge that crimes are about to be or have been committed, such lack of knowledge cannot be held against him. However, taking into account his particular position of command and the circumstances prevailing at the time, such ignorance cannot be a defence where the absence of knowledge is the result of negligence in the discharge of its duties. This commander had reason to know within the meaning of the Statute." If I may just briefly indicate what essentially appears to have happened with the Trial Chamber decision in the Celebici case. Essentially, the Trial Chamber in Celebici, if I understood the case correctly, decided that what we had, or what had happened was that as a result of the post World War II war crimes cases, "had reason to know," or the mental -- the knowledge element required for command responsibility included, as a matter of customary law, sort of a "should have known" standard, a standard similar to the one which we have been putting forward by the Prosecution in this case. But then when Additional Protocol I was drafted, for some reason the legal standard was narrowed; and then, however, they appear to concede that as time marched on and we had the Statute of the International Criminal Court adopted, then the meaning of customary law broadened again. But during the particular period of time when offences were committed in this case, you had a narrowed version of the scope of the knowledge standard as a result of the wording of Additional Protocol I. When one looks at the rationale for the Celebici Trial Chamber coming to that decision, they certainly paid a very great deal of attention to the negotiating record, to the travaux preparatoires for the Additional Protocols. It is our submission that, in fact, they paid too much attention to that negotiating record and that, in fact, it is, first of all, equally practicable to interpret the provisions in Additional Protocol I in a fashion which results in the same knowledge standard that we have put forward here, particularly when you read Articles 86 and 87 together, and even if that interpretation of Additional Protocol I is wrong, and we submit it is not, the customary law standard continued to co-exist with the provisions of Additional Protocol I. If I may give a particular example to substantiate that second aspect of our argument. As a result of the post-World War II war crimes trials, there developed essentially a doctrine that superior orders was not a defence to a war crimes charge. When Additional Protocol I was negotiated, there was extensive discussion about putting into that instrument a provision related to superior orders. Eventually the negotiators were unable to agree on a text. There is nothing in Additional Protocol I or Additional Protocol II, for that matter, which refers to the doctrine of superior orders. Having said that, no one, I would submit, has since suggested that well, because Protocol I didn't address superior orders, all of a sudden superior orders might become a legitimate defence again. The old customary law continued along because there was nothing in there. Now, here we've got a provision addressing -- or two provisions addressing command responsibility, after a fashion, in the Additional Protocols, but there was first, we would submit, a legitimate basis for interpreting Articles 86 and 87 together and to maintain sort of what can be regarded almost as a "should have known" standard. Secondly, there is -- it is also legitimate, we would submit, to argue that the old customary law continued to co-exist with Additional Protocol I, particularly bearing in mind that the Statute for the International Criminal Court also, for the most part, tends to adopt a standard somewhat similar to the one that we are putting forward here. That concludes my -- or our submissions with respect to the "knew or had reason to know" standard. Once again, Your Honours, I ask if there are any questions that you would like to pose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Fenrick, I would have one question to put to you. You mentioned the Blaskic judgement, and you said that it was spoken about negligence of the commander and absence of knowledge. According to you, and since you have also mentioned custom law, according to you, does this go under the due diligence doctrine, i.e., the doctrine which mentions this notion of superior responsibility in cases of negligence when there is an absence of action, when the necessary measures have not been implemented, the so-called due diligence doctrine as it is called by international law? This is a question I would like to put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that would essentially be our position. Our position is that if one is, to use the wording of Protocol I as an example, if one is to consider the scope of the knowledge requirement, it cannot be considered -- or cannot be assessed in the absence of the duty to inform. A military commander has in particular, as a result of Article 87 but also as a preexisting obligation, a duty to take all practicable measures to ensure that his armed forces comply with the law. As part of that duty, he must ensure that the forces are adequately trained. He must also set up some kind of a reporting mechanism, and he must make sure that that reporting mechanism actually works. The superior is not entitled to just stand there and say, "Well, I'm sorry, but I was concentrating on other things. I was busy engaged in fighting a war, I wasn't paying attention to what my people were doing to prisoners," or things like that. It is a part of the duty of this superior to be informed. It doesn't mean there is any kind of a strict liability standard here, but it certainly does mean that he or she is obligated to try and set up a system and make sure that a -- set up a reporting system, that is, and to make sure that that system reports or functions properly. If he or she does not do that and as a result does not become aware of information indicating an offence is about to be committed or has been committed, then, generally speaking, yes, he or she could be held criminally responsible for failing to carry out that duty, and determining the knowledge standard must be done at -- while bearing in mind the duty requirement, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Following on what my colleague said now, in answering his question, you mentioned that you are not invoking strict liability, but you would be basing all your negligence. Don't you think in that case -- I want to find out what is the borderline between the two notions, because wouldn't it be necessary in that case to prove the negligence, in specific terms, not to be -- not to remain within strict liability, I mean. Which would be your comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: I would -- I think that's accurate, Your Honour. I would suggest, however, that one can establish that negligence by circumstantial evidence in the same way as one could establish by circumstantial evidence that the accused or the superior must have known. In the Celebici judgement itself, there is, in the discussion of proof of actual knowledge by circumstantial means, a list of criteria that one might look at in order to determine, on a circumstantial basis, whether or not the accused actually knew of the offences being committed. I would suggest that evidence of that nature might also be sufficient to establish whether or not the accused should have known, within the meaning of the Blaskic decision, in the same way. One can, of course, also, if practicable, obtain information about the actual reporting systems that were available to the accused and those things that he set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think the time has come to take a break, Mr. Fenrick. You would have to add, would you not, to your answer to Judge Pocar, that the system that he should have set up would, in fact, have determined or found out that there were offences being committed. There would have to be a factual causal link between the failure to keep himself informed and being able to stop these things happening or to be able to find out that they had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: If I recollect my argument earlier, Your Honour, I said that not only must the reporting systems be set up, but one must -- it must be monitored to determine that it works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to prove that if it had worked, he would have found out. That's the point. But anyway, let's take the break now. We'll resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If it please Your Honour, I adopted Your Honour's invitation to speak to the Prosecution during the short adjournment. The net result is that on behalf of the appellant Mucic, we make this application: That insofar as his case is concerned and matters pertaining to his case, that there be no final determination by the Appeals Court until such time as we've had the opportunity to see and examine all of the documents that the Prosecution may wish to rely upon or may wish to adduce in this case or seek to adduce, and, thereafter, be permitted to make such application or raise such motion as is appropriate after having seen those documents. I am told that they are all in the hands of the translators at the moment. There are 12 translators working upon them, and most of the documents are no longer than the ones that have already been shown to the Court. So we're talking about two, three pages in the main. Nobody can give an exactly predicted time scale, or I think the Prosecution may have a better idea after this adjournment than they had before it, but I would simply undertake, on behalf of the appellant, to move as expeditiously as possible, as soon as those documents are available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, some time limit is going to have to be imposed upon the Prosecution assuming that we allow them to leave this option open, so that it would be more or less the same time for you, I would have thought, or at least to give us notice of an application to alter your grounds of appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, thank you, very much, Mr. Morrison. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think what we have seen this morning is the tip of what will turn out to be a very difficult iceberg to deal with. It seems to me that this Tribunal must take the position that there comes a point where every case ends. The situation that exists in the former Yugoslavia is such that it is entirely possible that in every case that is heard by this Tribunal, at some point following the Trial Chamber's judgement or the Appeals Chamber's judgement or somewhere in between as we have here, that somebody will discover some additional documents that could have been relevant in some way to the proceedings. That's the nature of these cases, especially considering the extraordinarily difficult task of securing documents from the former Yugoslavia. We all know that in every case that is before this Tribunal, that there are materials available somewhere in the former Yugoslavia that would assist a Trial Chamber in deciding the cases, but it seems to me in the interests of finality of this Tribunal's work, that there must come a time when you say, "That's it. We don't care if there are any additional documents," unless in the very extreme example that some document would appear that would show that someone is absolutely not guilty who had been convicted. There would be a substantial injustice that would simply need to be corrected. So I think it is unwise, at this point, for the Tribunal to allow this matter to remain open and go forward, because you would be setting a precedent that cases simply cannot end here, and I think they must end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You understand, though, that all of those considerations you put forward would be relevant to any decision which is made when the Prosecution seeks formally to tender this as fresh evidence or whatever use it wishes to make of this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I think, however, it's my duty on behalf of my client to oppose the Prosecutor's request, and I do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I just wanted to inform you that we have been informed by -- the first thing is the Translation has indicated, if it's relevant to your determination, that on Friday, June 23rd, would be, in their expectation, the date on which the documents would be translated. That's my -- so I think approximately three weeks. The 23rd of June is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is for 145 documents of two or three pages long.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's my understanding from the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: With 12 translators working on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: No. I think that was a bit of a misunderstanding and that may have been a problem in discussions with Mr. Morrison. The Translation Unit, as you know, is part of the Tribunal. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did nobody think of making photostat copies so that they could go to the translators earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: In light of the procedure that we follow, it took two days of 12 people. So there were only two days that it took, the Wednesday and the Thursday morning to have them indexed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There are times when bureaucracy does have to be put to one side, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The 23rd seems to me to be a very long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I can certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
