I can certainly make further inquiries if you wish, and I'll try and raise this after the lunch break to try and leave it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it might be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Unless you wish to hear from me on the comments of the other two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's what I called upon you for.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I was going to say. The first comment, simply, is that Mr. Morrison appears to be, at this stage, joining in the application of the Prosecutor, and has, it appears from his submissions this morning, indicated that in his view, the documents are substantially germane, as he indicated. That being the case, it appears that not only does he see the necessity for the proceedings to remain open, but it appears from the wording he used that upon his initial review on the face of them, they are, in fact, significantly influential or significantly important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, he has, of course, a ground of appeal directed specifically to command responsibility, and what he wants to do, as I understand what Mr. Morrison said, is to consider whether he can have these entered as fresh evidence in order to assist him on his arguments under ground 9, I think it is. It's a bit difficult to remember what Mr. Mucic's ground numbers are; they change so often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Ground 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So you would not oppose the delay of his ground being argued until they've had the opportunity to consider this material?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Maybe there's a misunderstanding between Mr. Morrison and myself on the application of Rule 115. I would submit that the Prosecution's position is that there are two distinct issues here. The first is whether there was an error committed at the trial level, which of course are to be seeking guidance of the Appeals Chamber, which includes of fact and errors of law. The second issue is the determination as to whether or not under Rule 115 additional evidence could have rendered the conviction unsafe. That's a separate issue which I would submit doesn't necessarily require this Court to actually take those documents and apply it to the present grounds of appeal. The grounds of appeal may stand on their own or fall on their own in light of the record before the Trial Chamber. The additional issue is whether, based on the facts before the Trial Chamber, including the new evidence, not making findings necessarily of -- complete findings of fact on them, but including the new evidence, that those new facts could have affected the verdict rendered. If that's the case, then the matter, we would submit, would be remitted back to the Trial Chamber. It's not that this Court then makes all new findings of fact with respect to the totality of the evidence at trial and a determination of findings of fact de novo on new evidence before it; it's just to reach the threshold that the conviction was unsafe and therefore is remitted back to the Trial Chamber. I see those as two distinct issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but if that one succeeds, then there's no need for us to determine whether the Trial Chamber made an error of fact based upon the material that was at the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, likewise, if you make a determination that they made an error of fact in the first place, you would send it back, remit it back for a new trial and wouldn't have to determine the other issues. So I see them as the same --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: -- with respect. Just with respect to Mr. Ackerman's comments, Your Honour, his comments about finality are appreciated and, in general, agreed with. But in our submission, that's why we have the Rules. The Rules themselves, in fact, set out what the finality is in relation to the proceedings before this Chamber, and Rule 115 specifically sets out the issue relating to finality, and as well as Rule 119 and Rule 120 for the review proceedings. So absent a determination of this Chamber that under Rule 127 an adjournment wouldn't be granted to file it, I would submit that the Rules, in fact, that we're attempting to apply determine the issue, and I think it would be, in our respectful submission, a little bit -- wouldn't be the correct result if these documents were found 5 days previously, which would make it within the time frame of 15 days, and they could be admitted simply for the sake of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, it's not the question of when they were found, but when you make an application.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: And whether due diligence was exercised, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But if we were to grant the Prosecution's application to leave its options open, there would have to be some very strict timetables imposed, and that is why I think, if I may say so, the Translation Unit's attitude is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One would have thought that these documents could be done so that we would see them by the end of this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'll certainly look into seeing whether that's possible, and I obviously agree with your comments about the need for a strict time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Excuse me for one minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just add something that I neglected when I was up a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I just needed to get a document. With respect to the -- two matters. First of all, I was informed by Mr. Huber, the case manager, that he has asked what the earliest possible date was, and it's the indication that the earliest possible date would be the 19th, that the Translation Unit has made it a priority, that it would take approximately one to two weeks to translate and then give themselves approximately one week to revise. I will once again confirm those dates, but that's just further information for you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think the Translation Department can do far better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'll certainly impress upon them the Chamber's concern. Secondly, with respect to the request for the disclosure of the documents immediately, the Prosecution just has a few comments in that regard. First of all, all the documents haven't been reviewed, obviously, as you're fully aware, and the Prosecution's concern, of course, is that there may be some material in there, sensitive or otherwise, that may have to be redacted. At this point in time, Your Honour, we don't -- the Prosecution doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: How about a rolling disclosure? In other words, you give them what you've done already, or your 12 investigators have got through, and you keep supplying them as they are processed through this bureaucracy that resides upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Assuming, of course, that the Prosecution is going to tender them under Rule 115, then we'll disclose them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was thinking really also of Mr. Mucic, who wants to know what the documents are from his point of view, as well as Mr. Ackerman's.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Once we're in a position to assess the ones that we have gone through, and if the Prosecution intends to rely on them and they don't have sensitive documents that don't need to be redacted, then yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You say you still haven't made up your mind even about the documents that these 12 people have been working on hopefully over the weekend, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. The documents that the persons have been working on were for the purposes of having them properly what's called indexed, for the purpose of having them given a proper identification number. There have been other persons working full time on having them translated, and those were some of the documents that we presented to you today. So to the extent that we are able, yes, Your Honour, we'll attempt to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Farrell, I'm sure you are well aware of the fact that the Appeals Chamber must at least have a list of your documents which you wish to submit as additional evidence. We cannot wait for you. We cannot wait for this machine of yours to produce documents one after the other. We have at some point in time to make a decision. Either we accept additional evidence, as is planned by Rule 115 of our Rules of Procedure, and that is for the Appeals Chamber to decide, and then we have to grant you an additional delay for the submission of these documents and we have to set a very precise time frame. But in order to do so, we must have a list of this additional evidence, even though these documents are not translated. You must try to act swiftly and you must try to give us a list of your documents of which you think that you may want to submit them as additional evidence, a decision which will in turn enable us to make a decision allowing you to tender them within the framework of Rule 115. And this decision can only be made if we have a list of these documents and at least an idea of what this document is all about. You don't need 12 people to achieve that, you don't need a hundred people to achieve that; you just need someone who is familiar with the B/C/S language and who is able to give you an idea of the content of the document so that you may decide whether or not this document is relevant and for you to decide whether or not you will choose to submit this document to us. This must be done within the days that remain during this week. Absent these measures, we cannot make a decision, an enlightened decision. You understand that. You cannot have carte blanche. You cannot have that kind of tool between your hands. I speak in my own name, but I would oppose such a decision that would basically give you carte blanche in order to make things easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. If there is a necessity, an order of this Court, we certainly will try to abide by it. The difficulty in giving you a summary at this stage is, quite frankly, that until there's a determination by the Office of the Prosecutor with respect as to whether or not we're even going to file a Rule 115, the Prosecution would take the position it's a little bit inappropriate to give you documents which bear on the guilt or innocence of the accused prior to it --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Farrell please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My apologies. The Prosecution would be of the view that it may be considered inappropriate to provide documents which may or may not go to the guilt or innocence of the accused prior to a determination whether we're submitting them. I'm not saying that the Court can't make its own determination. It's not going to be influenced in any way by the documents. It will determine the issue on the record before it at the trial, or if it admits it on the documents which it receives. I'm not saying it can't receive them; just that until we make a determination under Rule 115. In light of Judge Bennouna's concerns, at the break we'll try and make an effort to determine the best-case scenario with respect to the translation and with respect to providing the Chamber whatever material they think would be necessary to assist them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Farrell, I share Judge Bennouna's concerns about this. I cannot accept, frankly, that you have had 12 people just numbering these documents, and they've been working there for two days just so they can be indexed. They must have been forming some idea of what those documents contain. Now, those are the sorts of things that somebody from the OTP legal team should be looking at to be able to make a much better decision. You have five documents which, as you have outlined, may very well have relevance to the issues at trial. I don't say I've accepted what you've said, but you have put up a substantial argument as to their admissibility. Somebody with the material obtained by these 12 researchers should be able to then form a decision, and sometime during the course of this week, whether you are going to make the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You can't just sit back and let this thing roll on for some bureaucratic reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The Prosecution will make every effort by the end of the week to give you some indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but we want to be able to make a decision today as to whether the Prosecution is allowed to keep its case open on this. And I think that the decision has to be made today, otherwise you -- we don't want you filibustering to finish the day off and we have to make the decision tomorrow. So I think after lunch you had better come back with some more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll make sure I do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say with regard to the disclosure issue, it isn't, under Rule 66(B), just what the Prosecutor intends to use, but what might be material for the preparation of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I think that the Prosecution accept that. They just say that somebody within the OTP legal team has to make a decision on that rather than these researchers or investigators, whoever they are, who have been numbering the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just can see, with the experience that I have here, that we are weeks away from them deciding whether they're material to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, no, we're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Fenrick, may I ask you a question about the "reason to know or ought to or should have known." Is the position of the OTP different now that it has this material which may or may not go to the issue of direct responsibility or direct control? Because, you see, you've put this up as a purely academic exercise, as a matter of public importance for the Appeals Chamber to pass on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: It's my understanding, Your Honour, that it continues to not be directly related to any of the particular accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it remains a purely academic exercise? An important one, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: An important one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps, but nevertheless, it is purely academic and not related to the issues in this trial, or this appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FENRICK
utterances.text: If Your Honours have no further questions in connection with "knew or had reason to know," I would just like to briefly address the necessary and reasonable measures aspect of having the ability to prevent or punish, and essentially it's our understanding that a number of the Trial Chambers have decided that necessary and reasonable measures a superior may take are only those that are within his or her powers. That's primarily a factual matter and it's dependent on the circumstances of a particular case, and under some circumstances the obligation to prevent or punish may be met by simply reporting the matter to the competent authorities. If I might talk about sort of normal military practice very briefly, Your Honours. In many military legal systems these days, there is a very definite effort being made to insulate the military justice system from command influence, and in fact it would be most unlikely in most systems that you could say, "Well, this fellow is a commander. He is therefore entitled to punish the accused." Or, in the converse situation, "He doesn't have the power to punish, therefore he's not a commander or not somebody in a position of superior authority." It would be quite normal in many systems to have the military judiciary, or whatever judiciary is functioning, insulated from the command system so that all that a commander could do would be to start an investigation in motion or to pass a complaint to a different level of authority. And the necessary -- the fact that a general, for example, is not entitled to summarily punish a particular perpetrator is irrelevant in these cases. It's all a matter of circumstance. And that's all I have to say on that issue, Your Honours. If there are any further questions. Those are all of my submissions related to the command responsibility issue, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, now, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise, Your Honour. I'm not obviously getting to the point of incurring your favour by this, but the grounds of appeal in relation to 7(3), as indicated in the outline -- and I apologise. This may not have been made clear at the beginning -- related to a number of issues under 7(3), and the outline indicates that the law on command responsibility is with respect to the issues Mr. Fenrick addressed and then that there are other grounds of appeal in the brief: Ground 2 and ground -- and an additional issue regarding -- ground 2 and 3 regarding the Prosecution appeal brief. Those two grounds were not addressed by Mr. Fenrick. He spoke about the law. And the second ground relates to the application of the law to the facts in this case and the Prosecution's request for a remedy, which is the substitution of a verdict of conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this what you're saying, that you are going to follow Mr. Fenrick?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: With your permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It had not been made clear to us that you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- and I would have called upon you otherwise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Moran. I have now had the opportunity of looking at the document. It was handed in to us. And it is made very clear there, so you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I should have indicated that at the beginning, or maybe we could have had Mr. Fenrick address that at the beginning to make it clear. In light of the time, I'll try and make my submissions as precise as possible, or concise as possible, while still speaking at a reasonable rate. The ground 2 that's in the brief is an application of the law, as submitted by Mr. Fenrick, to the facts in this case. There's two options as a result of a finding, if this Appeals Chamber finds that there was an error of law. The first is that if it finds on the facts as found, as a result of the application of the correct test, that there could be no other reasonable conclusion than guilt, the Prosecution would ask that they submit a substituted verdict of conviction. If the facts as found either do not address some of the elements necessary for a finding of guilt, or are such that they are equivocal, then if there is an error of law, the second option is to remit it back to the Trial Chamber. The Prosecution's position on ground 2 is that if you look at the facts as found, applying the test which the Prosecution submits is the correct one, submitted by Mr. Fenrick, then the result would be a substituted verdict of conviction. As you know, Mr. Fenrick made a submission that one of the errors submitted by the Prosecution in relation to the test applied is that of superior/subordinate relationship. And as he indicated, there were three elements to the relationship: One was that the superior have an effective control over persons committing the violations; secondly, that effective control is articulated as being the ability, the material ability, to prevent or punish the commission of the offence; and thirdly, that that control can be de facto or de jure. In the Prosecution's submission, the Trial Chamber erred in its conclusion with respect to Mr. Delacic on superior responsibility because it appeared to focus on the necessity of a chain of command. It appeared to focus on the necessity of that there has to be a command structure, rejecting the Prosecution's submission that in certain circumstances there may very well be a superior who has a substantial influence that could bring about, or who has the material ability to bring about, the prevention or the punishment of crimes, or that there may be circumstances where he's not in the direct chain of command himself, though has a position which could exert that influence as well. The bottom line being that the Trial Chamber's reliance on the need for a chain of command, and specifically some -- what appears to be some direct link or direct chain of command, caused them, in the Prosecution's submission, to negate two possibilities. These two possibilities which the Prosecution submits reflects the correct approach are, one, that a person may still be found liable where they are not in a specific delineated chain of command with identifiable subordinates; or two, there may be circumstances where the superior is in fact in a non-command function where that superior may incur liability. And these two possible circumstances would require that the superior/subordinate relationship should not be defined by the Appeals Chamber in a narrowly circumscribed scribed manner. Mr. Fenrick has referred to the hostages case, the Hirota case, and the Muto case as examples where the World War II case law supports that there may be -- it's not that it's necessary, and you have to look at the circumstances of each case, but there may be circumstances where a person in a non-command position may be held criminally responsible. In the submission of the Prosecution, it's important to recall that the purpose of the command responsibility, and the purpose of the sections as set out in the Additional Protocols, is to prevent war crimes from being perpetrated and to punish those who commit them. Article 68(1) talks about the general obligation to repress or suppress breaches, and the additional commentaries at page 1007 indicates that the importance of this provision cannot be doubted. It would appear, in the Prosecution's submission, somewhat illogical if you find that there are a commission of war crimes, if you find that a person has sufficient authority or responsibility such that they could prevent them, but they are not found liable because there are no direct subordinates. With respect to the Hirota case; the Muto case, the staff officer who is not in a command position, these are examples where in the special circumstances of those cases, and it may very well not occur very often, but in the special circumstances of those cases, where they can effectively or materially affect and bring about the prevention and punishment, they shouldn't be subject to prosecution simply because they claim that they have no direct subordinates. That position, as taken by Mr. Fenrick, requires an understanding, when dealing with Mr. Delalic, of the facts. There is one issue, though, I'd like to address before proceeding on the facts in relation to Mr. Delalic, and that's the scope of the Appeals Chamber's ability to assess the evidence at trial, the evidence on the Trial Record, and make its own determination on the basis of that evidence. To be fair, in the Prosecution appeal brief at paragraph 3.34, the Prosecution submits that the Appeals Chamber can do one of two things: It can rely on the facts as found or it can rely on any evidence not rejected by the Trial Chamber. It's that second aspect that I would like to address very briefly right now. There's a certain difficulty in the judgement, in our respectful submission, in that the Trial Chamber makes certain findings of fact but then doesn't proceed any further. For example, in the evidence with respect to Dr. Grubac, the Trial Chamber acknowledges that Dr. Grubac was released and that the release order was signed by Mr. Delalic. There's no reference in the evidence of Dr. Grubac to Dr. Grubac's testimony that he was informed that Delalic will release him from the prison. There's no reference to that in terms of an actual finding of fact. It's in the transcripts. There's no reference to the testimony of Dr. Grubac's wife, that she went to Delalic himself, specifically Delalic, to have her husband released and he was subsequently released. The difficulty is that there seems to be evidence that accepts that Mr. Delalic had a role to play and signed the document, the release order, but doesn't make any comment to the rest of the evidence on that specific issue. Now, in fairness, the Trial Chamber found that he was signing the documents only on behalf of someone else. The Prosecution, in an attempt to bring to the attention of the Chamber this other evidence which doesn't appear to be contradicted, put in the submission that the Appeals Chamber could actually make new findings of fact on any evidence that was not rejected or not contradicted by the Trial Chamber. After the Tadic Appeals Chamber's decision and after this Appeals Chamber's decision as well in Aleksovski, the Prosecution now takes the view that the Appeals Chamber cannot intervene and make findings of fact on evidence on the record. In a situation where there is to be an intervention on the facts, it's the Prosecution's submission that the Appeals Chamber be permitted to intervene on factual matters in at least three circumstances. The first is where no reasonable person could have taken the view of the evidence that was taken by the Trial Chamber. This is a clear error of fact standard, and it was articulated both in Tadic and Aleksovski, both in Tadic in the majority and in the separate opinion of Judge Shahabuddeen, and it basically is a reasonableness standard for a determination whether the factual findings at trial constituted an error. The converse, of course, is that where there is only one reasonable conclusion to be drawn from the evidence and the Trial Chamber did not draw the only reason conclusion from the evidence, that would constitute error of fact as well. The second would be that the Trial Chamber failed to take into account relevant facts or took into account irrelevant facts, and the third would be that they applied the wrong legal criterion to the determination of the significance of the facts. In the Prosecution's submission, these are examples where the Appeals Chamber can intervene, and these three examples are taken from the Tadic decision, but that the Appeals Chamber generally must accept the facts as found by the Trial Chamber and that the Appeals Chamber generally does not exercise a de novo function in relation to evidence presented at trial. When the parties are alleging an error of fact, and in this case the Prosecution is alleging the facts as found should have -- the only reasonable conclusion is that the Trial Chamber should have found him guilty once the Appeals Chamber applies the correct legal test is a standard of unreasonableness and not, as we submit in our brief, that the Court can look at any evidence not rejected by the Trial Chamber. I think that's fair in light of the decision as well in paragraph 167 in Aleksovski, where the Appeals Chamber states that, "Unless it is safe to infer that the Trial Chamber formed a particular view of the evidence beyond what was expressly said, the Appeals Chamber cannot draw an inference from this evidence," and the Prosecution obviously is bound by that decision of the Appeals Chamber in Aleksovski. Therefore, applying the law, the applicable law, as the Prosecution submits by Mr. Fenrick, to the facts in this case, my reference will be specifically to facts found in the Appeals Chamber's decision. With respect to Mr. Delalic, the facts by the Appeals Chamber seem to be clear. Sorry, the Trial Chamber. My apologies. He started in the Konjic municipality as a civilian. He had no official position when he arrived in the civilian or military structure, but by the beginning of May he was receiving authorisation to act on behalf of the state to procure weapons and equipment in other state, that being Croatia. The Trial Chamber found that he was a well-placed, influential individual. Within one month of being -- apparently one to two months of being in Konjic, he was appointed the coordinator in the region, and he was empowered to directly coordinate the work of the defence forces of the Konjic municipality and the War Presidency. He engaged in regular intervention designed to facilitate the work of the War Presidency with different military formations. He signed a document regarding opening the railway line between Pazaric and Jablanica. The Court found, in fairness, that this was a formal acknowledgment of the involvement of the coordinator but that, in fact, according to the evidence one of the brigadiers who testified, his signature was needed to have the order effected quicker. Mr. Delalic coordinated and directed the proceedings of a meeting of the military investigation commission on a particular occasion in June 1992. The Court concluded that he was simply acting on behalf of a superior command, but the position being is that he is acting in this capacity. He's meeting with members of the commission, he appears to be directing the proceedings, he reads out an order to them, and he explains how they are to conduct interrogations of detainees in the prisons. This was during a period of time that he was the coordinator, when he allegedly had no de jure or no de facto authority with respect to the prison, but he was performing a function in relation to the interrogation and classification of prisoners in Celebici. With respect, this has nothing to do with his alleged facility as a coordinator dealing with logistics. He signed release orders in July 1992, as found by the Trial Chamber, on behalf of the head of the investigating body of the War Presidency. Once again, this is again while he was a coordinator, while he was allegedly someone who was involved in the procurement of weapons and dealing with logistics. In this situation, the Trial Chamber finds that he was given authority by the head of the investigating body, and he was given the authority as a result in relation to the release of prisoners. Once again, this has nothing do to do with being a coordinator. He was assigned the commander of TG-1, as found by the Court, as indicated by my friend correctly. Presumably he took over the function around July 30th. I think that would be a direct reading of the judgement. And that that was signed by the president of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He had contacts with the International Committee of the Red Cross, who were conducting visits to the prisons and reporting on the treatment, and it's once again submitted that this has nothing to do with his assigned functions as found by the Trial Chamber with respect to him being a commander. And once again, it's respectfully submitted that it's because the Trial Chamber approached the legal test of requiring a chain of command, and if the subordinates in the prison, being the prison officials Mr. Mucic, Mr. Delic, were not in a chain of command back up to Mr. Delalic, he couldn't be found guilty. The evidence also accepted by the Trial Chamber is that he signed two orders directing action to be taken in the Celebici prison: one on August 24th, 1992; one on August 28th, 1992. These were issued by Mr. Delalic as commander of Tactical Group 1, and they were directed to the armed forces supreme command staff of Konjic and copied to the Celebici prison administrator. These orders concerned the functioning of Celebici prison camp, and in the order he indicates that the commander of the Konjic armed forces is responsible to him for the prompt and effective implementation of these orders. It also indicated that there was a direct order to Mr. Mucic to establish a commission of three members to undertake the interrogation of prisoners. Once again, the Court looks at this and says that he was acting on behalf of someone else and that he had no direct command authority over the prison. It is submitted that Mr. Delalic, though maybe not found to be in the direct chain of command here, when applying the test as to whether or not he was someone who was in a position of authority to meet the effective control test such that he could have had influence over the persons committing the crime and could have been -- had the material ability to prevent and punish. It is submitted that the facts clearly show that he is not simply someone who is involved in logistics or assisting in lifting the siege of Sarajevo; he acts on behalf of the War Presidency, he acts on behalf of the supreme command in Sarajevo, he acts on behalf of the investigating commission with respect to prisoners, he issues orders with respect to the functioning of the Celebici prison, he indicates that a commander of an armed forces in Konjic is directly responsible to him to implement the order. The only reasonable inference, it is submitted, is because he then has to report back, if we accept the Trial Chamber's reasoning, he has to report back to the supreme command in Sarajevo, if we accept the reasoning that he's acting on their behalf. He issues orders on behalf of the investigative bodies, he reports orally in writing to the War Presidency, and as commander he reports to Sarajevo. Based on these very facts as found by the Trial Chamber, it is submitted that there are two bases for the reasonable conclusion that he performs a function such that he has sufficient control or authority or powers of substantial influence to exercise the material ability to prevent or punish. If he is not in a specific chain of command, he is similar to the other cases referred to by Mr. Fenrick in the sense that he is in such a special position that he has links with all the parties. He has links with the War Presidency, he has the ability on behalf of the supreme command in Sarajevo to issue orders, he reports back to the supreme command in Sarajevo, and he has the authority to communicate and intervene in relation to all of them. As a result of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: As a result of this specific position and someone who is granted authority by the higher command, it is the Prosecution's position that those facts demonstrate he had control. The other -- the only other -- the other possible basis on which the Prosecution indicates that there is an inference is that he, in fact, when you look at this first scenario, he is, in fact, in the chain of command. He, in fact, is the link. He's the link between the supreme command in Sarajevo and orders to the Konjic forces. He's the link for the orders on August 24th with respect to the Celebici prison. He's the link with respect to the investigating commission when they can't, as found by the Trial Chamber, they can't undertake the releases of prisoners. He's the link with the supreme command when there's a meeting of the investigative commission to give them orders. With respect, he is in the chain of command. He, in fact, is one of the links in the chain of command, though his link is not a direct link as the commander of the prison, as found by the Trial Chamber. In light of those factual submissions, it is the submission of the -- factual conclusions, it is the submission of the Prosecution that applying the test, as submitted by Mr. Fenrick, this Court could come to no other conclusion that, in fact, Mr. Delalic did have the requisite ability to prevent and punish and was a superior. The submissions regarding the appropriate remedy in this regard are that if the Appeals Chamber accepts the Prosecution's submission that the Trial Chamber erred in the test it applies and in applying the correct test, as the Prosecution submits, to the facts as found concludes that the only reasonable conclusion is that of guilt, it's submitted that the Appeals Chamber reversed the judgement and revise it by substituting a verdict of conviction. If, on the other hand, the Appeals Chamber accepts the Prosecution's submissions that there was an error in the test it employed but feels that based on the facts as found it's not in a position to revise it to enter a verdict of guilt, it's submitted that the appropriate remedy would be to remit the matter to the Trial Chamber. Thirdly, the Prosecution has included within its submissions the secondary argument that the Trial Chamber erred in excluding evidence. This is in the brief. You'll see that the Prosecution submits that on the facts as found --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do I have an objection at this point? I had perhaps wrongly assumed that the Prosecutor had abandoned this point. They had asked in their brief that the -- this Chamber give them the opportunity to present witnesses and evidence on that point before the Chamber, and having not pursued it any further following that point, having not made any application to bring witnesses before the Chamber as they indicated in their brief they were going to do, I was of the opinion they'd abandoned it. They did not raise it at the Status Conference as an issue that they were going to raise during these arguments. During the Status Conference, we went through all of the issues that were appropriate to be argued, and the Prosecution never mentioned that this matter would be brought before the Chamber during these arguments, and so I, therefore, assumed that they had abandoned the point by not pursuing it after they had raised it in their briefs. They didn't make any further application to this Court to bring the witnesses before this Court to prove those documents. So I think it's totally improper now for them to, in that context, raise this issue that they clearly had abandoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes? It is a little surprising, I must confess. I read that only the other night and noted that there had been nothing produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Well, maybe the fault lies with the wording in the reply brief, but that section only goes to the remedy, not to the abandonment of the ground of appeal, as I understand it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you say that the Trial Chamber wrongly excluded evidence, we have to know what the evidence is, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The evidence is before you. The question was the appropriate remedy if you found that they erred in law in excluding the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Was this only documents? I didn't realise it was limited to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. There was documents and three witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The issue is an issue of an error of law. The issue is whether or not the Trial Chamber applied the correct test for the admission of rebuttal or fresh evidence. If they applied the incorrect test and it's an error of law, then the Trial Chamber erred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but this is another one of these solely academic matters unless we know that if they had not erred it would have affected the result, and we can't decide that without knowing what the evidence was that you sought to tender, other than the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I apologise for the misunderstanding, but quite clearly the documents are before you. All of them are before you. They're attached as three appendices to the appellant's brief. What the remedy that the Prosecution submitted in its first appeal brief was that the Appeals Chamber could call all the witnesses, make new findings of fact, and not have to send it back to the Trial Chamber. That's different than having the evidence before you -- obviously you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, I see your point, but is this for some academic exercise then, simply to say that the right of the Prosecution is to lead evidence in reply even though it is not in reply or even though it was a matter that should have realised by it during its case-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The ground of appeal is that the Trial Chamber erred in the exclusion of evidence, that it erred in law with respect to rebuttal or fresh evidence, and the documents are pertinent to a determination of the liability of Mr. Delalic. One of the documents, for example, is that the hand -- what the Prosecution has called the "handover document." It's on November 17th, it's signed by Mr. Delalic, and it hands over authority from the present commander of the prison, Mr. Mucic, to the subsequent commander of the prison, Mr. Delic. It's the Prosecution's submission that these documents are germane to the issue before them and could have affected their understanding and the approach -- not only the approach taken but the facts as found. The remedy that was proposed, Your Honour, with respect to -- in the brief was that once the facts -- once there was an error determined and once there was a determination obviously that it wasn't a harmless error because the documents and the witnesses are relevant, after that determination is made, then the next question is: What's the remedy? The normal remedy would be that the matter would be remitted back to the Trial Chamber, in my respectful submission. The -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: The proposal in the Prosecution's appeal brief was that instead of having it remitted back to the Trial Chamber for the sake of 23 documents or 21 documents and two sets of documents and three witnesses for a complete new trial that took 18 months, that the Appeals Chamber would have the authority to actually, once the determination was made that there was an error and it wasn't a harmless error, that the documents were relevant to a determination before the Trial Chamber, that one option was to have the Appeals Chamber hear the evidence, make findings of fact, and then determine on those findings of fact in relation to all the other findings of the Trial Chamber. As a result of the Tadic decision and subsequently indirectly in the Aleksovski decision, the Prosecution understands and takes the view that the Appeals Chamber is not a de novo finding of fact function, that its role is circumscribed to a court of review, and that was indicated and was the position of the Prosecution in Tadic, in light of the need to safeguard the right of appeal of an accused and the Prosecution, that this should go back to a trier of fact. It may have been unclear, and I apologise if it was on behalf of the Prosecution, but it's in the remedy section and it deals with the appropriate remedy if there is a finding, as indicated, of an error of law and it wasn't a harmless error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, is this what you are now saying: You say that there was an error of law, the documents which are attached to the submissions will demonstrate that it was an error of law which caused harm to the Prosecution's case, and, therefore, you want a new trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're not going to see anything more of the evidence other than the documents which are attached to the appeal brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, with all respect, Your Honour, the Prosecution, without requesting an opportunity to amend their briefs or anything of that nature, has all of a sudden today, without any notice, basically taken a completely new tack. What they had requested in their briefs was that witnesses be brought before the Trial Chamber and that then the Trial Chamber should consider whether or not these materials should be admitted. Now, clearly they did claim that the Trial Chamber erred in not admitting them either in rebuttal or otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is material that you've answered in your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have answered it in my submissions, yes, I have, and then it became clear to me that they had apparently abandoned their option. Now what they're asking is that you consider it as for the purposes of whether or not there ought to be a new trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. They're limiting the nature of the relief which they seek, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think adding to the nature of the relief that they seek, that they didn't request in their brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, they have elsewhere. I can't recall whether it was in this particular section, but they have elsewhere sought it in the alternative, that the Appeals Chamber decided or send it back to the Trial Chamber, and I don't see that you would be taken by surprise by the alternative form of relief being raised here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The real surprise, Your Honour, is that it was never mentioned at the Status Conference; it's not part of the schedule, not any of the issues that were scheduled for us to hear. They didn't mention it at the Status Conference, and I firmly believe that they had abandoned their efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't think you're correct on that. One of the grounds of appeal which we have listed is the one where, as I recall, the argument says the Trial Chamber erred in ruling that they could not lead this material in reply or as fresh evidence, and they put up a fairly brave submission that the Prosecution should not be restricted, as it always seems to have been restricted, to putting in its case in its case-in-chief, unless it is something which it could not have foreseen. That's clearly there under these grounds of appeal which have been listed for argument today. So on that basis, I don't think that you're really taken by surprise as to the argument. If you are taken by surprise in relation to the nature of relief which they seek, that is matter which I'm sure we will allow you to put something in writing if you can't deal with it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can deal with everything today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sure you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just a short question, Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You summed up Mr. Delalic's position in your words that he had the authority to communicate and intervene in relation to all parties. That was the summing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just perhaps for further information, you concluded that he had the -- then he had the requisite ability to prevent and punish. He was almost a mid-man. He was always between people. Would that be enough to prevent and punish or to report? What would be your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. The position is that as the mid-man, as someone who is essential as the link in this chain and as someone, as is evidenced by the documents, that they are to report right back to him, that he is in a position where he can have a substantial -- I mean obviously it's a substantial influence, the material ability, and that he can by his ability to either take actions himself by indicating it, or if he is not found to be somewhere within the chain of command, he has the authority to report to the appropriate -- he has access to all the appropriate -- if the command is the Territorial Defence in Konjic, he has the authority, the links, and the reporting mechanism to them and he is given the authority. If he has to report -- if he can't -- if there is no recourse of action there, he has the ability, obviously, and the links with the supreme command in Sarajevo, who have on two occasions, we know, given him the authority to act on their behalf. With respect to the investigative commission, there is evidence that he is -- it appears on the evidence, quite clear from the Trial Chamber, that he is asked to proceed and direct a meeting of the investigative commission and hand over a fax to them indicating what their steps are to do. Obviously he is used as the conduit, as the Trial Chamber says, but not as the conduit without knowledge. You can't have the responsibility of being -- I'm sorry. You can't have the function and power of being some type of person in authority and not have the responsibility that comes with it. And that responsibility, in our respectful submission, is to report. Since he is not, as found by the Trial Chamber on the facts as found, Your Honour, since he is not in the direct chain of command over the subordinates, he would, similar to the other cases we referred to, take steps to report to ensure that there will be steps taken to prevent or punish. That would be the submission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Farrell, one question for you. I go back to this issue of new evidence. You said, in English, the Chamber erred in excluding evidence, i.e., you said that the Chamber choose not to take into account a certain number of documents of evidence and that it erred in that sense. Is that in any way linked to your position on the legal aspect of the issue? If I followed you correctly, when you don't apply the right legal standard, the Chamber errs because it has not chosen to take into account a certain number of facts. Is that exactly what you said or am I misinterpreting you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: I think that's a fair submission, that the error in law by the Trial Chamber with respect to the test to be applied to the documents resulted in them excluding documents which they should have considered and which should have been part of their factual finding process. I think that's fair, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Yes, I see. Thank you very much, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.text: Mr. Farrell.

utterances.text: Your Honour, regarding the information that you had requested, the case manager, George Huber, is still trying to ascertain some information. utterances.text: But may I say this to you. You're obviously going to need the documents to be properly translated for the purposes of your motion. utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. I was going to address that second. I have spoken with some of the investigators and other members of the team. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You have provided us with five documents with proper translations. You were able, actually, to give a brief description of them before you got the translations.

utterances.text: Of course, the application itself would have to have the proper documents translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: We will undertake to get as many of the summaries as we can in light of the original --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, that would bring forward the time that you have to make up your mind whether you want to proceed with this application quite considerably, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: It would if we can get the summaries and review them and present them to you, we would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But you have 12 people working on it, and they have been working on it, as I understand, since last Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Judge Hunt, I should maybe clarify. Once again, I apologise if it's unclear. The 12 people are not investigators. They are people within the evidence unit that input, transmit, and summarise documents for identification purposes. They are not anybody who knows about the case nor are they translators. utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, now, bearing in mind that for the purposes of giving you an extension of time, we only need to have a description of this material, succinct, but, nevertheless, a description, when do you suggest that you would be ready to give us that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that the Prosecution needs a variation of the time limit imposed by Rule 115 for a motion to present fresh evidence in the hearing of this appeal, and without intending to lay down any hard and fast rules as to what must be shown in such a motion, the Appeals Chamber believes that it is reasonable to require the Prosecution to file a document by first thing Thursday morning, the 8th of June, in which it states whether it proposes to file such a motion, and if so, it describes succinctly the evidence which it proposes to tender; it identifies just how that evidence creates the significance possibility that the Trial Chamber, acting reasonably, would have convicted Mr. Delalic if that evidence had been before it; and it specifies the period within which, acting expeditiously, it will file that motion. In the meantime, the Appeals Chamber will treat the Prosecution's appeal against the acquittal of Mr. Delalic as remaining open. If no such document is filed within that time, the Appeals Chamber will treat the Prosecution's appeal as closed. If such a document is filed, the Appeals Chamber will issue a scheduling order for the future conduct of that motion. The Appeals Chamber emphasises that the Prosecution's obligations of disclosure under Rule 66 and 68 are still owed to Mr. Delalic, and for that matter, to Mr. Mucic, and it expects full such disclosure to take place at the time when the motion is filed or within such further time as may be allowed. Yes. Well, Mr. Staker, it's your turn, I believe. Yes, Mr. Yapa.

The next stage, there are two grounds of appeal of the Prosecution, grounds 5 and 6, which will be dealt with by Mr. Christopher Staker, and thereafter, I presume that it will be the counsel for Mr. Mucic on ground 7, who will make the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's now ground 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Staker.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: May it please the Chamber. The Prosecution's fifth ground of appeal relates to the Trial Chamber's finding that Hazim Delic was not liable as a superior under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Mr. Delic was accordingly acquitted of the charges in the indictment to the extent that they charged him with responsibility as superior for acts committed in the Celebici prison camp. The relief sought by the Prosecution in relation to this ground is set out in paragraph 8.1, subparagraphs 4 and 5 of the Prosecution appeal brief. The Prosecution seeks the reversal of the acquittals on the accounts there mentioned. In relation to the relief sought, I would also refer the Chamber to paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask Mr. Staker to speak a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You're also being asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would refer also to paragraph 6.22 and 6.23 of the Prosecution appeal brief, which makes clear the point, of course, that to the extent that any subordinate of Mr. Delic was found not guilty on any account, that Mr. Delic couldn't be found guilty as a superior in relation to that count. In this case, we submit the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Delic was the deputy commander of the Celebici camp. The relevant parts of the Trial Chamber's judgement in which these findings were made are set out in paragraphs 6.12 to 6.14 of the Prosecution appeal brief, and we understand that this finding of fact is in fact conceded by Mr. Delic in his response brief at paragraph 245, and we therefore submit that this appeal proceeds on the basis that Mr. Delic was the deputy commander of the Celebici prison camp. In essence, what the Trial Chamber found was that Mr. Delic was not criminally liable as a superior because there was no evidence that he lay in a specific chain of command between the guards committing the crimes and Mr. Mucic, who was the -- who was found to be the commander of the prison camp. The Trial Chamber therefore appears to have considered the possibility that there was a chain of command going from the guards directly to the prison commander that bypassed the deputy commander. As the Trial Chamber said, and I would just quote briefly from paragraph 810 of the judgement: "After having reviewed the relevant evidence before it, the Trial Chamber finds that the Prosecution has failed to establish beyond reasonable doubt, that Hazim Delic lay within the chain of command in the Celebici prison camp, with the power to issue orders to subordinates or to prevent or punish criminal acts of subordinates. Accordingly, he cannot be found to have been a "superior" for the purposes of ascribing criminal responsibility to him under Article 7(3) of the Statute." We submit that it's apparent from this passage that the Trial Chamber treated the superior responsibility of Mr. Delic as turning on whether or not he lay within a specific chain of command between the guards and Mr. Mucic. This reflects the Trial Chamber's finding at paragraph 647 of its judgement, where it said that "The Trial Chamber is unable to agree with the submission of the Prosecution that a chain of command is not a necessary requirement for [sic] the exercise of superior authority." Now, my colleague Mr. Fenrick has presented the Prosecution's submissions on the legal principles governing superior responsibility, and these are also dealt with at length in our written submissions. For the reasons that have been given, the Prosecution's submission is that superior responsibility arises from the power to control the perpetrators in the circumstances, and can arise even in the absence of a direct chain of command between the accused and the subordinate. However, it's also our submission that even if the legal test applied by the Trial Chamber were accepted as the applicable test, that the Trial Chamber incorrectly applied that test to the circumstances of this case. Mr. Fenrick also presented the Prosecution's submissions that superior responsibility can arise on the basis of de facto as well as de jure authority. In that connection, I would also make reference to the recent decision of the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski appeal, at paragraph 76, where the possibility of de facto superior authority was recognised as a possibility in the case of civilian commanders as well as military commanders. This possibility was dealt with in particular at paragraphs 354, 378, and 376 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. Perhaps it's unnecessary to quote those paragraphs at length, but the formulations used in those paragraphs include wording, for instance: "It is necessary that the superior have effective control over the persons committing the underlying violations ...in the sense of having the material ability to prevent and punish the commission of these offences." And at paragraph 736 it's again stated that: "It will be further observed that whereas formal appointment is an important aspect of the exercise of command authority or superior authority, the actual exercise of authority in the absence of a formal appointment is sufficient for the purpose of incurring criminal responsibility. Accordingly, the factor critical to the exercise of command responsibility is the actual possession,or non-possession,of powers of control over the actions of subordinates. Hence, where there is de facto control and actual exercise of command, the absence of de jure authority is irrelevant to the question of a [sic] superior's criminal responsibility for the criminal acts of his subordinates." So the test enunciated by the Trial Chamber itself in this case was a test of effective control or of actual exercise of authority or of material ability to prevent and punish, and not a test of formal or de jure chain of command. So in relation to the specific case of Hazim Delic, the question is: Did he have de facto or de jure effective control or actual exercise of authority over the guards in the camp? The evidence and findings of fact in respect of this are dealt with by the Trial Chamber beginning at paragraph 798. Paragraph 798 and 799, there the Trial Chamber refers to evidence that the detainees regarded Mr. Delic as the commander or superior of the guards and evidence that the guards referred to Mr. Delic as "the boss." At paragraph 803 there is set out further evidence that Mr. Delic gave orders to the guards, that the guards obeyed him and even feared him, and that Mr. Delic would occasionally severely criticise or shout at the guards. Paragraphs 804 and 805 set out evidence that he ordered guards to mistreat the detainees. In relation to the incident referred to in the former of those two paragraphs, paragraph 804, the Trial Chamber found that it had not been proved that the beatings had been ordered by Mr. Delic, but in relation to the incident referred to in the second of those two paragraphs, paragraph 805, two witnesses testified that Mr. Delic ordered or commanded the guards in the collective beating, and the Trial Chamber made no finding that this evidence was unreliable. Further evidence is also referred to in paragraphs 801 and 802, although this evidence was given by Mr. Delic's co-accused, Mr. Landzo, on which the Trial Chamber found it did not rely unless supported by other evidence. Furthermore, as I already said, it was found that Mr. Delic was the deputy commander of the prison. In other words, after Mr. Mucic, Mr. Delic was the most important and influential person in the camp with organisational functions in respect of running of the camp, which were set out in paragraphs 807 to 809 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. The Trial Chamber concluded that all of this evidence was insufficient to establish Mr. Delic's superior responsibility. Its specific finding is at paragraph 806 of the judgement, where it says: "In conclusion, this evidence is indicative of a degree of influence Hazim Delic had in the Celebici prison-camp on some occasions..... However, this influence could be attributable to the guards' fear of an intimidating and morally delinquent individual who was the instigator of and a participant in the mistreatment of detainees, and is not, on the facts before this... Chamber, of itself indicative of the superior authority of Mr. Delic sufficient to attribute superior responsibility to him." The Prosecution submits that this finding is unreasonable in the sense that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached this conclusion on the evidence before the Trial Chamber. The evaluation of the evidence in relation to Mr. Delic can be contrasted with the approach that the Trial Chamber took in relation to Mr. Mucic, whom the Trial Chamber found on the evidence before it to be the de facto commander of the camp. In evaluating this evidence, the Trial Chamber said, and I would quote here from paragraph 750 of the judgement: "It seems inescapable, from the testimony of all the detainees that they acknowledged Zdravko Mucic as the prison-camp commander. The detainees came to this conclusion because Hazim Delic called him the commander, or because Mr. Mucic introduced himself as the commander, or because his behaviour towards the guards was that of a commander. The Trial Chamber considers the last of these factors the most significant for the purposes of ascribing superior authority. Concisely stated, everything about Mr. Mucic contained the indicia and hallmark of a de facto exercise of authority. Even in the absence of explicit de jure authority, a superior's exercise of de facto control may subject him to criminal liability for the acts of his subordinates. Where the position of Mr. Mucic manifests all the powers and functions of a formal appointment, it is idle to contend otherwise." That's the end of the quote. Now, if similar reasoning is applied to the evidence in relation to Mr. Delic, what inference must be drawn? We have the person who is the deputy commander of the camp. He's perceived by the detainees to be the commander of the guards, he gives orders to the guards, he's obeyed by the guards, and he's referred to by the guards as "the boss." The Prosecution submits that the only reasonable inference that the Trial Chamber could have drawn from this evidence was that de facto, if not de jure, Mr. Delic, as the deputy commander of the camp, exercised actual authority over the guards. The conclusions that the guards only obeyed his orders because they feared him as an intimidating and morally delinquent individual is, in our submission, not a conclusion which any reasonable trier of fact could draw from the evidence. In any event, even if subordinates do fear their superior as an intimidating individual, this is irrelevant to the superior's status as a superior. The issue here is whether Mr. Delic, the deputy commander of the camp, in fact exercised effective authority over the guards, de facto or de jure, and it's submitted that the only reasonable conclusion is yes. Whether or not it was officially or formally the duty of the deputy commander of the camp to exercise that function, de facto the deputy of the commander did exercise that function, and there was thus a de facto chain of command between the guards, Mr. Delic, and Mr. Mucic. For Mr. Delic to be responsible as a superior under Article 7(3) for the crimes committed by the guards in the camp, it's also necessary to establish that he had reason to know of these crimes and failed to prevent or punish them. This is dealt with in the Prosecution appeal brief at paragraphs 6.18 to 6.21. It's conceded that because the Trial Chamber concluded that Mr. Delic was not a superior for the purposes of Article 7(3), it declined to make findings on these issues. That was stated at paragraph 810 of the judgement. However, the Prosecution submits that on the findings of fact made by the Trial Chamber in the case as a whole, no reasonable conclusion could have been drawn by any trier of fact other than that these elements of superior responsibility were satisfied, and on this basis the Prosecution submits that it's possible for the Appeals Chamber to substitute verdicts of guilty on the Article 7(3) counts in the case of Mr. Delic. Unless the Chamber has any questions in relation to that ground of appeal, I propose to move to the Prosecution's ground 6. May it please the Chamber. The Prosecution 6th ground of appeal relates to the Trial Chamber's finding that Mr. Delic was not liable as charged in Count 48 for the unlawful confinement of civilians in the Celebici camp. Mr. Delic was charged under both Article 7(1), and Article 7(3) in respect of this crime, and although this ground of appeal has been included in group 1 of the issues for the purposes of oral argument, in fact the Prosecution's principal argument in relation to this ground of appeal is based on Article 7(1) in particular. The Trial Chamber found that civilians were unlawfully confined in the Celebici camp, and it further found that Mr. Mucic, the commander of the prison, was guilty of their unlawful confinement. Mr. Delic, the deputy commander, was similarly charged but was found not guilty for the simple reason that the Prosecution had failed to demonstrate that Mr. Delic was in a position to effect the continued detention of civilians in the Celebici camp. That finding was made at paragraph 1144 of the Trial Chamber's judgement. It said in that paragraph that because of that circumstance, Mr. Delic cannot be deemed to have participated in the offence. The Prosecution submits that as a matter of law, this reasoning contains a plain error. It assumes that only persons who had the authority to order the release of detainees from the camp could be liable for their unlawful confinement. In other words, the Trial Chamber treated the power to effect the release of the victim as an element of the crime. The Prosecution submits that this is not an element of the crime of unlawful confinement of civilians. The unlawful confinement of a large number of civilians, as occurred in this case, is obviously something which no individual can effect single-handedly. The continued detention of so many people could only be effected by a body of camp personnel and others acting in concert. As noted in the Prosecution appeal brief, any detainee who had attempted to leave the camp would have been prevented from so doing not by the camp commander but by one of the camp guards. The most immediate cause of each detainees confinement and the most immediate obstacle to their liberty was thus the camp guards, and the reality is that all of the victims could have simply walked out of the camp at any time if the guards hadn't been there to prevent them from so doing. I submit there may be an analogy with the kind of situation that arose in the Erdemovic case, where an individual subordinate is ordered in that case to kill numbers of victims. Now, it may be that the accused was acting under superior orders and it may be the accused had no choice over who the victims would be and who would be killed and who would be released, but that doesn't affect the criminal liability of the accused. We would submit here that if an individual camp guard is standing at the door of a building in the camp, and by standing there is preventing civilians within that building from leaving, that individual camp guard is detaining those civilians, which is the actus reus of the crime of law of unlawful confinement of civilians, and we would say that the guard would be found guilty of that crime, even an individual guard, provided that the guard had the necessary mens rea. To have the requisite mens rea, the individual guard or other member of the camp personnel, in our submission, would need to know that the detainees in the camp were being unlawfully confined and must, nonetheless, have continued to participate in the illegal confinement of those people. By saying that the individual guard must have known that they were unlawfully confined, I don't mean that the guard must necessarily have known what the law is because ignorance of the law is not universally recognised as a defence to a criminal charge. An accused committing grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, in our submission, should not escape criminal liability merely because the accused says that he or she has never heard of the Geneva Conventions or doesn't know what their provisions are. This is a matter which is dealt with in more detail in paragraphs 8.12 to 8.18 of the Prosecution response brief. In our submission, it's enough that the individual guard knows, for instance, that the detainees are civilians associated to the opposing party in the armed conflict, knows that they pose no threat to the state, and knows that they are only being detained as a collective measure and not as a legitimate security measure, and if that's established, the Prosecution submits that there is the necessary mens rea. If an individual guard has this knowledge and, nonetheless, continues to participate in the detention, he or she may be criminally liable. As I say, superior orders are not a defence to a crime under the Statute. The Prosecution submits that the position of the Prosecution and that of Mr. Delic on this issue may, in fact, not be all that far apart. It is conceded that the individual personnel, particularly those at the lowest level in the camp, may have little knowledge of the individual circumstances of the detainees and may not be in a position where they could reasonably be expected to have any idea of the particular circumstances or background to why the detainees happen to be there. And on this issue, I would quote directly from paragraph 265 of the response brief filed on behalf of Mr. Delic, at Registry pages A2393 to A2392. This paragraph says and I quote: "At some point, it becomes clear that confinement is unlawful, just as it becomes clear that a military order is unlawful. Clearly, the confinement in the Auschwitz concentration camp in [sic] World War II was illegal. Guards who unloaded trains, separated men from women, oversaw the selection process and herded the sick and old to the gas chambers could not believe that they were engaged in lawful activity. "Just as clearly, the warden of a prison who accepts an inmate based on a judgement of a competent court is acting legally even if that judgement is later overturned on appeal. The instant case falls somewhere between the two extremes". Well, even accepting that, the question then is: In this case which side of the line does Mr. Delic fall? The evidence of Mr. Delic's knowledge on which the Prosecution relies is set out in 7.16 of the Prosecution appeal brief and paragraph 7.5 of the Prosecution reply brief. The Prosecution submits that on the basis of that evidence, the only reasonable conclusion that could have been drawn by the Trial Chamber is that Mr. Delic, like Mr. Mucic, was aware that the civilians detained in the camp were detained on the basis of their ethnic background and their detention was not a legitimate security measure, and to the extent that the detention of any of the detainees might have been originally justified by any security concern, that no proper inquiry had been undertaken into their status to ensure that those civilians who could not be lawfully detained were immediately released. Those are the Prosecution's submissions into Mr. Delic's liability under Article 7(1). In relation to his liability under Article 7(3), the appeal, to that extent, would lie on a finding that there were subordinates of Mr. Delic who committed the crime of unlawful confinement of civilians. So, of course, to that extent, it's dependent also on the outcome of the fifth ground of appeal relating to his status as a superior. It also depends on a finding then that there were individual guards within the camp, of which Mr. Delic was the superior, who also had the requisite degree of knowledge that would make them criminally liable for such a crime so that Mr. Delic could incur criminal liability as a superior. The Prosecution concedes that the Trial Chamber made no express finding to the effect that there were individual guards who had knowledge of the facts that the civilians there were being detained in circumstances which would render that detention unlawful. The Prosecution submits, however, that on the basis of the evidence as a whole, the inference must be drawn that at least some of the guards must have been aware of this. To give one example, in paragraph 1269 of the Trial Chamber's judgement, the testimony of one witness is referred to, which is not rejected by the Trial Chamber, "that at one stage Mr. Delic walked into Hangar Number 6 and told us that we were [sic] all detained because we were Serbs." There thus appears to be no suggestion that the circumstances of the detainees within the camp was a matter that was secret or confidential in any way. Given also the composition of the detainees, for instance, the fact that it included elderly men of 60 or 70 years of age, and in respect of that I would refer to the Trial Chamber's judgement at paragraphs 823, 839, 850, and 982, and given the way that the detainees were being treated, it's submitted that the only reasonable inference would be that the guards, or at least some of them, were aware that this was a kind of collective measure aimed at the detainees on the basis of their ethnic background and not a legitimate security measure. However, if the Appeals Chamber doesn't accept that this is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn in respect to in the evidence before the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution would request that the acquittal on Count 48 be reversed to the extent of the alleged liability under Article 7(1) of the Statute even if not under Article 7(3) as well. Those are the Prosecution's submissions on the Prosecution's sixth ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Staker. Now, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I might have a second to get organised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I'm Tom Moran, and along with Salih Karabdic, I represent Hazim Delic in this case. I would first like to talk about command responsibility, and, frankly, I think both sides have written more on command responsibility than the Appeals Chamber wants to read, and it's been pretty well briefed. What I'd like to do is just clear up, I think, some ambiguities we may have had and be available to answer questions for the Court. Command responsibility, simply put, holds a commander or a person liable for the criminal acts of others, even if he has no connection with those acts.
