It's a vicarious type of liability that's different from a personal responsibility which could be on a commander or any other person who orders a crime, aids and abets it, takes part in it, encourages it. The doctrine of command responsibility traditionally has been a rapier, something used at a point target. The Prosecutor wants to turn it into some kind of a two-handed broadsword to hold people criminally liable when they can't find any other way to do it. The theory behind the legal doctrine is based on the nature of command. The first real command responsibility document I found is cited in paragraph 40 of my brief. It's a regulation adopted by the United States Continental Congress in 1775, holding commanders responsible for the acts of their subordinates on a march if they looted, stole chickens, things like that. It said if they didn't punish them, then the commander would be held liable just as if he committed the offence. The basis of military command is that the commander is responsible for everything his unit does or fails to do. Command is the personal authority to enforce the will on subordinates. Commanders can delegate that responsibility -- or that authority, rather, but they can never delegate the responsibility. The responsibility remains with the commander, not the Chief of Staff, not the first Sergeant, not the chaplain, with the commander. In fact, The Hague convention and the first three Geneva Conventions from 1949, when they're talking about what is a legitimate belligerent, requires that these units be commanded by a commander responsible for his subordinates. Literally on my way to the airport to come here, I picked up a book just to read on the aeroplane, an autobiography written by an Admiral of the United States Navy in World War II, and there's a little something that he said in there that I thought I would read to the Appeals Chamber. When he became commander of a ship, one of his subordinates issued an order which, if it wasn't illegal, was really stupid and could have got the Captain relieved, and it was put into effect. The minute he found out about it, he stopped it. He says in his autobiography: "Of course, I knew nothing about this order and would never have sanctioned it if I had known, but it happened on my ship. It was my duty to indoctrinate all officers of that ship so they wouldn't think of doing any such stupid thing, to organise the ship so such an order could not have been issued without my knowledge, and to supervise what went on on the ship closely enough so that I would soon find out if such a blunder were committed. For failure in all these respects, it would have been my duty to take the rap." That is command, Your Honours. The scope of a commander's legal responsibility under a command-responsibility theory is coextensive with his authority. The broader the commander's authority, the broader his duty. For instance, the hostages case and the high command case which Commander Fenrick [sic] talked about earlier today made a distinction between an occupation commander who has the full authority of the state to exercise authority within a given area and a tactical commander. For instance, in the high command case, Field Marshall von Leeb was held by the court not to be responsible for abuses of prisoners of war because he had no responsibility in that area. Commander Fenrick [sic] and I seem to disagree on whether or not Articles 86 and 87 are codifications of the traditional Rule. However, we do agree that you generally have to look to customary international law, especially the post World War II cases, the high command case and the hostages case, to determine when a person is liable under a command-responsibility theory. The Prosecution relies specifically on three cases to talk about command responsibility based on an influence theory. Two of them came out of the Tokyo tribunals. One was the conviction of General Muto and the other was the conviction of the Foreign Minister Hiroto. Let me just read something that was written by a commentator about that, about the Tokyo Tribunal. It says: "Because the Tokyo decision stands alone, its presciencial value is ambiguous. It is unclear, on the basis of the decision, whether one could conclude the political and bureaucratic leaders have exactly the same responsibility as do military leaders for the acts of their subordinates. One reason why command responsibility doctrine may differ for military commanders and the others is that military commanders do exercise command. They have control over subordinates and a rigid hierarchical system with disciplinary powers and the authority to order subordinates. The scope of this military authority includes the power to order subordinates to risk their own lives, most bureaucratic leaders do not wield the same type of life-and-death authority." I agree with that completely. When Mr. Fenrick wrote that in 1995, he was absolutely right. He's still absolutely right today. I think that the Tokyo decision is ambiguous, and its -- even if it is not, it stands alone, when you look at the other case law and the other customary law on command responsibility, for holding non-commanders, such as General Muto, liable on a command-responsibility theory. Clearly non-military people can be held liable on a command-responsibility theory. I think there is no question about that. But it is going to have to be someone who has -- who is exercising powers over subordinates which are substantially similar to those of military commanders. That is going to be the rare civilian indeed. It's going to be people like high-ranking police supervisors, possibly high-ranking bureaucrats that have policy-making powers and have the powers to have substantial disciplinary action against their subordinates. Probably the best example of the superior is in the Aleksovski case. He's the warden of a prison, he was appointed the warden of a prison, he had the authority over everything in that prison, and it didn't make any difference whether he was military or civilian so long as he had that kind of personal authority. Let's talk about what a superior is not. A superior is not necessarily someone who just holds a higher rank than the person committing the crime. An example would be the Chief of Staff in a military unit. We know from the high command case and the hostages case that the Chief of Staff is not criminally liable on a command-responsibility theory even for his own subordinates on the staff. The Court says he's not liable because he lacks command authority. Yet that Chief of Staff, by the very nature of his rank, is going to be the senior person to many or most of the unit's commanders. He will clearly be senior to every company commander in the division and probably every battalion commander and likely every brigade commander or regimental commander. Therefore, you have to look for the existence of that personal power, that personal authority; not delegated authority, not the authority that is delegated from a commander to a staff officer or a subordinate; the authority that is inherent in the status of command. I think every one of us that's ever been a staff officer in any army at some point in our lives signed a document for the commander. I know I did. And most of the time the commander never saw it. But it was his order. He was responsible for it. Now, if I made a mistake, I was responsible to him, but I did not have any command authority. All I had was what the colonel gave me. It's the same in any military. "Superior" doesn't mean someone who, through some sort of force of personality, exercises some kind of unofficial control over other people in a unit or in a bureaucracy. It can't be that way for two reasons: One, it could relieve that commander, that de jure commander, of his responsibility. He could sit there and say, "I couldn't control Ratko Mladic. He was out of control. He is a stronger personality than I am." That command responsibility has to reside with that commander, and no one else. As you can tell from reading my briefs, I think I have -- the biggest problem I have with the Trial Chamber's decision is this concept of de facto commander, and the reason is that I'm not sure what one is. If a de facto commander is someone like Aleksovski, who was a civilian that was exercising the same kinds of authority as a military commander, without the title, then that's not a problem. And you would also see, I think, de facto command more in an internal armed conflict, where a rebel force would not have the law to appoint a de jure commander. Whoever is in command there is going to be a de facto commander pretty much by definition. But when you start applying this to people that may be exercising delegated authority or may, through sheer force of personality or other means, have influence, have control over troops, you're muddying the entire concept. Influence. I'm not sure what is sufficient influence. This is a concept that I don't know how you develop a legal test on. I don't think anybody does. How do I know when this person had sufficient influence, doesn't have sufficient influence, to be held liable on a command responsibility theory under the Prosecutor's view of the law? Clearly, again in a military unit, the most influential person in that unit other than the commander is probably the chief of staff. He sits at the commander's right hand. He is in charge of the day-to-day running operations of the staff, which in turn, do all of the things that the commander doesn't have time to do. And yet that influential person is not liable under a command responsibility theory. If it's just powers of substantial influence, I'll give you an example of one where you would have to have substantial influence; that is, the staff judge advocate of a military unit, the commander's lawyer. If that lawyer doesn't have influence, and substantial influence, on the commander, the commander ought to fire him and get somebody who does have influence, whose advice he does trust. And yet under the Prosecutor's view, the staff judge advocate, who by definition is a subordinate with no command authority, could be the commander's superior if he exercises that kind of influence. That's turning the entire process on its head. In criminal law we need to have some certainty, and we should construe criminal laws narrowly. Under this influence theory as put forward by the Prosecution, I don't know how you could have any certainty in the law on when someone is criminally liable based on influence. The Prosecutors themselves say you have to look at it on a case-by-case basis. If you have to look at it case-by-case, there is just a complete lack of certainty. Knowledge is really not a factor in this case, the knowledge available to a commander and the knowledge that a commander has. The Prosecution, I think, wants the Appeals Chamber -- somebody was talking about academic exercise. It may have been Judge Hunt, it may have been one of the Prosecutors. I don't think that's something that the Appeals Chamber needs to write on. But if you do, I think the starting point is Article 7(3) of the Statute. And if I could digress just slightly to talk about the status of the Statute, exactly what the Statute is, it's my position that the Statute does not create crimes, does not define crimes. Those are defined by other laws. The Secretary-General made that clear in his report to the Security Council. What the Statute does is create a court to try allegations of violations of certain laws, in certain times, in certain places, and give that court jurisdiction. The words in Article 7(3) are "knew or had reason to know that the subordinate was about to commit such acts." That is different from the standard in the high command case. In the high command case, the Court held that a commander has the duty to get reports, and if the reports aren't sufficient, he's derelict in his duty and that's not going to be a defence. I think there's no question that a commander on any level is imputed with all of the knowledge in his headquarters. That's the only way that the system and the law can work. A good example of that is the My Lai cases, which I cited at some length. The company commander knew that there was a massacre going on, and as soon as he knew about it, he used his best means of communications to stop it. That's the kind of knowledge that Article 7(3) has, either imputed knowledge, knowledge that would allow this person to understand that there are crimes going on. I don't think Article 7(3), which vests the Tribunal with jurisdiction on command responsibility cases, authorises you to look further than the knowledge that was actually available to the commander and what he could and should have been able to do with that knowledge. Going over the Prosecutor's argument just a little bit, since -- punish. Different commanders have different abilities to punish. In the militaries that I'm familiar with, non-commanders do not have the ability to impose punishment in a legal means. They may be able to take them out behind the barracks and beat them up, but they don't have the authority to impose legal sanctions. Mr. Fenrick talked about a doctrine called command influence. Command influence -- and I wasn't going to talk about it, but I think I probably should, because it came out here. It had to do with a commander's ability to interfere with military justice, the discipline within the military. With the militaries that I'm familiar with -- and I'm sure not going to tell you that I'm an expert on every military in the world -- it's the commander that decides whether or not someone will be court-martialled, someone will be tried for a crime. It's not the staff advocate, it's not the military judge. It's the commander that convenes the court and decides what the charges will be. The doctrine of command influence simply says that that commander cannot influence the result. The commander cannot get what the members of the court, de jure, if you would, and say, "Vote guilty," "Vote not guilty." That's illegal command influence. The commander has legitimate influence, legitimate authority, the power to decide whether or not charges will be filed and whether or not this Prosecution will go on, another reason why command responsibility, criminal liability, is limited to commanders and no one else. Chain of command. The chain of command is simple. It's a chain from commander to commander to commander, from the highest level to the lowest level. People who are not commanders are not in a chain of command. It's just that simple. Therefore, people who are not commanders don't -- should not be held liable on that command responsibility theory. Mr. Ackerman is going to talk about this at some length, but let me -- I've noticed in my notes the Prosecution talked about a link, one person being a link between the investigating commission, the supreme command, the municipal government in the Konjic area, and therefore he had influence and he was a superior within the meaning of the doctrine of command responsibility. Just because a person is a link does not make him a commander or a superior. A liaison officer is a link. The radio telephone operator is a link. The fellow that drives the Jeep carrying the messages is a link. The chief of staff is a link. The chief of staff's job is to put all this information together for the commander so that the commander can understand what is going on. Mr. Staker was talking about directly involving Mr. Delic, that we agree he was a deputy commander. We do agree that he was a deputy commander at the times relevant to the indictment. And in fact, sometime after the events alleged in the indictment, he became the commander for a short period of time. There is nothing in the indictment, nothing in the judgement, which is relevant to his time as commander. The fact that he is perceived by the detainees as the commander of the guards is absolutely irrelevant to anything. The fact that he could give orders to the guards does not necessarily show he was a commander. There is this delegated authority that the Chief of Staff has, that other people have, that we talked about in command. The fact they called him boss, I don't think that makes any difference. When you're deciding the issue on Mr. Delic, one of the things I think the Court needs to recall is that in the high command case, dealing with the Chief of Staff for an army group, the Court specifically said that the Chief of Staff is not responsible for his own subordinates on the staff, the people that report to him, and the reason he was not held criminally liable for their acts is because he was not a commander; he lacked command responsibility. He was, if anything, a supervisor. Unlawful confinement. Then I'm going to sit down. I'm not going to take too much more time here. The unlawful confinement count centres not on the conditions of confinement but the fact of confinement itself. I don't know of a civilised society -- and as soon as I say that, I'm sure there will be one. Someone will point one out to me -- where the people that run gaols, that run prisons, also make the decisions on who goes in and out of that prison. Clearly, Mr. McFadden, the commander of the UN Detention Unit, does not go behind an order from this Court on whether or not someone should be incarcerated. If a judge on this Court, or the authorities here, make a mistake on the existence of probable cause, Mr. McFadden doesn't care. All he cares is that the legitimate authorities, in an order that is not obviously on its face illegal, ordered him to take custody of these people. The same situation applies in the Celebici prison. These people that were held in the Celebici prison were taken into custody after a battle with the legitimate forces of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the government that was recognised by many countries in the world, the government that had a seat in the General Assembly. It was in the middle of a war. Clearly the authorities have the right to take those people into custody, at least long enough to sort it out. But who sorts it out? Is it the gaol guards or is it some other authority that sorts it out? I submit to you that it's some other authority other than the gaol guards. The confinement of those people there was not obviously illegal. The Prosecution says that all that's necessary to show mens rea is that the guards knew that there were civilians being confined, they're part of an imposing side, and they're held as a collective measure. Well, there is more, I think, that's required than that, as -- when I had my brief read back to me, it's correct. If you're a guard at Auschwitz, you know that you're engaging in illegal confinement. But how about confinement of people who have, or at least there's probable cause to believe, have engaged in armed conflict with your legitimate government? Does a prison guard at that point have some kind of criminal liability if the legitimate organs of the state don't promptly investigate or if they don't properly investigate? I don't think so. I don't think there is any more criminal liability than there would be on any other gaoler who accepts prisoners, detains prisoners, on the order of a court or some other authority, and then on the authority of that court releases them. Your Honours, I promised to keep this short, and I don't know if I've kept it short enough. But unless there's some questions from the Appeals Chamber ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can I just get your position clear? You are not seeking to support the Trial Chamber's decision that the customary law had been altered by Additional Protocol I; you simply say that this Tribunal has no jurisdiction because of the limitation you see in Article 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to knowledge, as to knowledge only, which in my view is not an issue in this case. And anything that the Appeals Chamber would write would be pure dicta. But that is my view of it, that the limitations that are imposed in the Statute are limitations on the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. And I'll give you -- there could be good reasons for that, Your Honour. It very well could have been that the Security Council decided that some people, given the resources that are available, remembering that at the time that the Statute was passed, there were only 11 Judges, two Trial Chambers and the Appeals Chamber, that there's a limited number of people that can be tried by this Court, and that limitation on jurisdiction could be a way of limiting the number of trials that would come before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would include, would it not, the suggestion that we should be only trying the small fry and not the big fish, if I've got the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you may have turned it around, but that is -- I somehow don't think that in the Secretary-General's office, when the Security Council was considering establishing the Tribunal, that they thought about some of the people that have been tried here, which is not to say that there should be, you know, just carte blanche you try the defendants that you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, but your suggestion, as I understand it, is that we should not be trying anybody for superior authority unless there's some -- they fall into a much narrower area than the customary law permitted, but we should be trying the people who are the actual perpetrators, in other words, the smaller fry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm saying on command responsibility is that those commanders who are in command and have their subordinates commit crimes should be tried, and if the Prosecutor can prove that they knew or had reason to know that a crime had been committed or was about to be committed, they didn't stop it or they didn't punish it. I'm just suggesting, Your Honour, that that is somewhat narrower than the standard set up in the high command case, requiring reporting, and if the commander does not design proper reports, holding him criminally liable on that basis. It's just that the information where you could at least draw an inference is there. He knew or should have known, so that he can't exercise deliberate ignorance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Moran, I have a very specific question. It has to do with the distinction between the de jure superior and the de facto commander. The Prosecutor has made the distinction saying that finally what counts in respect of responsibility is the effective power of the superior and not his legal position or his judicial position. In order to understand this effective power and to evaluate it, it says this comes -- this ordinarily means that one has to look at things on a case-by-case basis. Apparently you have rejected that notion, the proposal to evaluate things on a case-by-case basis, saying that this does not show certainty. [In English] "Complete lack of certainty if one has to look on a case-by-case basis." [Interpretation] That's what you said. I don't see how one can personally examine somebody's effective power without this being on a case-by-case basis. The general rule is that there's effective power, that is, the power that one actually has, somebody about whom one knows that is giving orders, that he's perceived as a superior, and this can be proved only by looking at things on a case-by-case basis. Therefore, my question is to know whether you mean that you are against the proposal which says that responsibility depends upon effective power. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me try and clarify that. Let me think for a second. But my basic position is this: that authority in a military setting comes with command, and when you start blurring the distinction between a commander and someone who is not a commander, you start blurring the law. I think that de facto command, and where you look at effective authority, is probably much more relevant in a civilian situation, where you're deciding: Is this civilian bureaucrat or this civilian leader liable on a command-responsibility theory? And even there you're going to have some -- you're going to have to look at some kind of effective control but the control that he has also under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, but you are familiar with the doctrine of the de facto agent as developed in the Tribunal's case law and in the Nicaragua case at the International Court of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The de facto agent, who is not necessarily somebody who has any type of legal jurisdiction in any official way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I think we're here talking about apples and oranges, if you would, and I know that you don't think so, but one has to do with the responsibility of a state exercising influence and control over its agents. For instance, what the United States exercised over the contras in the Nicaragua case. And that can make something an internal armed conflict, an international armed conflict. But when you start talking about a command-responsibility theory, every commander has agents. He just can't do everything himself. He's going to have a staff. He's going to have an aid who makes sure that he gets where he's supposed to be with what he needs when he gets there. He's going to have a Chief of Staff. All these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think I've got my answer, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you think that the command responsibility theory is limited to military personnel or does it extend to the political arena as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Clearly, Your Honour, it extends to the political arena. I don't think there's any question about that. I think that it's a little more difficult to apply in the civilian arena, and the reason it's more difficult to apply is you don't generally have, in the civilian world, the indicia of authority and the ability to impose one's will on one's subordinates that exist in the military. A military commander can say, "Private, take that hill or I'll send you to gaol." A superior, a supervisor in a corporation can't say that. All he can do is fire you. So you have to look at those indicia of authority and the ability to impose his will in the civilian arena. And I think it's a much more difficult thing to do, which is why the commentators generally talk about civilians with military command-like authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There is another question, but I think we better take the break. But before we adjourn, I should have announced earlier this morning that we will take the group 3 grounds of appeal after group 4. It seems to be a more logical way of looking at it. So we'll go group 4 and then group 3. That will obviously be sometime tomorrow. We'll adjourn now until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Moran, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to follow further your reasoning concerning what you said about the commander's capacity to punish or to prevent. You said, and I'll even try to quote you, you said the commander has to have influence or power and to be able to file and prosecute any action. Now, I quite understand that as far as punishing is concerned. He has to have, in fact, the means to prosecute. Then my first question is: Does the fact that he is -- of course, you are for the de jure commander, not for de facto.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. Consider granting that, would the fact that he is a de jure commander imply automatically or at least have some kind of prima facie appearance that he can pursue the punishment or is it an extra -- it's addition, he has to prove that, although he is a de jure commander, we have to prove that he has got the means to prosecute?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my view, and this is just going to be on the view of the militaries that I'm familiar with, it is inherent in the position of commander that he has the authority to order a case prosecuted, to convene a court-martial. That division commander is going to be the general court-martial convening authority. He decides whether or not to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: He has the inherent power. So really you do not mean to add it as an extra condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I wouldn't think so, Your Honour, unless you've got a situation where there was a military where a commander did not have that, and I would think that would be more in the way of a defence to a failure to punish allegation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm glad you explained that to me. I thought it was not inherent in his power, it had to be proved, because you were rather forceful in this argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Now, that is with the military commander. Clearly a civilian superior is not going to have that type of authority. It's not going -- he might have the authority to fire someone from their job or to reassign them to a different position or something like that, but he is not going to have the authority that a military commander would have to put somebody in gaol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to mention that Article 7, paragraph (3), speaks of taking the necessary and visible measures to prevent such acts or to punish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Would that also apply to preventing? I mean, would that exonerate him from attempting at least to prevent, saying, "All right. Since I cannot prosecute, I should not attempt to prevent"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think that the two are two separate duties on that commander. One, he has the inherent duty as a commander to see that he accomplishes his mission, whatever his assigned mission is, within the realm of international law. He has to do that. He has to organise his unit, he has to supervise his unit in such a way that he accomplishes his mission with an eye towards preventing violations of the law. However, if they occur, and they do occur, we all know they occur no matter how careful someone is, then he has the duty to punish. But reason that he has the duty to punish is because that prevents the next one. That if a commander does not punish a violation of the law in this case, then he is almost encouraging his people to commit future crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So this is inherent in his position as a de jure commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It comes with the job, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: We don't need to prove it. And anyhow, even if he proves that he cannot prosecute, the duty to prevent remains intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Clearly, Your Honour. Remember this, the Statute and customary international law does not say "prosecute," it says "punish," and commanders have in their abilities other ways other than formal convening of a court-martial to prosecute. There are plenty of ways that a commander can punish one of his troops without convening a court-martial, as I'm sure you can imagine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna, I think I did not answer one of your questions well, and I thought about it over the break, so if I could try to do it. You were talking about the lack of certainty, and where I was thinking about lack of certainty was this concept of influence, that when does someone have the influence to stop crimes? At what point do they have that? That's what I was talking about when I was talking about lack of certainty, and I don't think I made that clear enough to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very succinctly, Mr. Moran. The question of absence of certainty in law deals with the rule of law itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does not concern the consequences drawn from the rule of law or the characterisation of a specific fact on the basis of the rule of law. It certainty has to do with the rule of law itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but you also have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certitude of the absence of certainty has to do with the rule of law itself, and that's why -- well, the rule of law is dependent on the state of customary law itself --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But it has to be certain enough that I can advise my client, be it the commander or whoever, that, "If you do this action, you're acting within the law, and if you do that action, you're liable to find yourself in The Hague."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, or elsewhere. If there are no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, is it Mr. Kuzmanovic or Mr. Morrison who's going to commence for Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to be speaking on factual argument for command responsibility on behalf of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Are you going to start?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if you'd like, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Whichever you prefer, Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. May it please the Court. I didn't know whether this is the beginning of the end or the end of the beginning relative to this case, so in the grand scheme of things, I'm going to just plunge ahead. The Court, through Judge Hunt, has made it clear to us that it did not want to hear us -- recitation of the briefing and it wanted to keep our arguments rather succinct, and I will endeavour to do both. It is the position of the Defence here of Mr. Mucic that as far as command responsibility is concerned, the Trial Chamber chose to adapt insufficient evidence in concluding that he was the de facto commander for the entire time period set forth in the indictment. It is our belief that its reliance on evidence cited in the judgement is unreasonable, and based upon this unreasonableness, the Appeals Chamber can substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber pursuant to the Tadic and Aleksovski cases. It is arguable that his status as commander could be said to be extended from July forward. The Trial Chamber, in our view, unreasonably backdated that de facto command to May. The standard of review was set forth in both the Tadic and the Aleksovski cases, I believe, on factual finding. The Appeals Chamber in Tadic found that factual findings or findings that should stand is that the standard is unreasonableness, that is, a conclusion to which no reasonable person could have reached. It is only where the evidence relied on by the Trial Chamber could not reasonably have been accepted by any reasonable person that the Appeals Chamber can substitute its own finding for that of the Trial Chamber. It's contained within paragraph 64 of the Tadic judgement of 15 July 1999. Although the Appeals Chamber has to give a margin of deference to the Trial Chamber's evaluation of the evidence presented at trial, the Appeals Chamber can overturn the Trial Chamber's finding of fact where the evidence relied on could not have been accepted by any reasonable Tribunal or where the evaluation of the evidence is wholly erroneous, and that comes from the Aleksovski judgement, 24 March 2000, paragraph 63. In addition to the arguments presented in the various briefs, we will focus -- or I will focus on the reasons why the Trial Chamber's conclusion that Mr. Mucic was commander in at least May, June, and July of 1992 was erroneous. And I think I agree with what was defined earlier by Mr. Farrell, I believe, on what Article 7(3) entails with respect to command responsibility and those elements. And I also think that the Aleksovski judgement in paragraph 70 is applicable here, and we really don't disagree with it; that is, anyone, including a civilian, may be --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you're reading, I'm afraid, Mr. Kuzmanovic, you do speed up. It's a very natural habit which we all have. So if you could just, when you're reading, take it slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, and I apologise to the translators. Paragraph 70 of the Aleksovski judgement states, and I quote: "Anyone, including a civilian, may be held responsible, pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute, if it is proved that the individual had effective authority over the perpetrators of the crimes. This authority can be inferred from the accused's ability to give them orders and to punish them in the event of violations." It went on to find that, "The appellant had effective authority over the guards as shown by his issuing orders to them and the availability to him of means to report to superiors the situation in the prison, including incidents of mistreatment of prisoners." I think the key language to focus on is "effective authority," what constitutes effective authority. Now, the indictment, paragraph 20, alleges, among other things, that Mr. Mucic was the commander of Celebici prison camp beginning from approximately May to November 1992. That's as specific as the indictment gets. His authority was, at least according to the indictment, derived by being appointed by Zejnil Delalic, whom the Trial Chamber had acquitted. The Chamber has not reconciled Delalic's acquittal with the source of Mucic's authority. Instead, the Trial Chamber, in our position, and we hope in the Appeals Chamber's position, used unreasonable testimony from witnesses to attempt to legitimatise its finding that he was the de facto commander from day one. The Trial Chamber itself acknowledges in paragraph 736 of its judgement that "Formal appointment is an important aspect of the exercise of command authority or superior authority." In that same paragraph, the Trial Chamber also emphasised that "The factor critical to the exercise of command responsibility is the actual possession or non-possession of powers of control over the actions of subordinates." Now, until today we have not had an opportunity, although we have argued in the past, that the formal appointment of Mr. Mucic had never taken place until approximately the end of July 1992. And I'm sure you're aware, having sat through many different cases, that the value and importance of what an appointment means, the fact that a document has been signed, the fact that a document has been stamped, the importance attached to orders and appointments, up until today we have had nothing that we have argued to show what in fact that appointment was, and obviously that's something that's not in evidence and I won't discuss it any further. But I think what the Trial Chamber has done to try and impute de facto authority to Mr. Mucic to the beginning, in May of 1992, is to use instances of his mere presence in Celebici to be proof positive of exercise of command. The testimony pointed out by the Trial Chamber in paragraph 739 of the judgement was, "At all times the de facto authority in Celebici prison camp was Mr. Mucic." Unfortunately, as Mr. Moran discussed, the Trial Chamber gave us no guidance on what de facto authority truly is and how it's defined. I think the only way Justice Potter Stewart of the US Supreme Court gave a definition once of what pornography is. He said, "I don't understand it, but I know it when I see it," and that perhaps is what the Trial Chamber has done with de facto authority. We have argued extensively that the date of his actual appointment and authority is critical in this case. And why? Why is it important to establish a date of his command? Why is it relevant? Simply because many of, if not most, of the bad acts that occurred in Celebici camp took place in May, June, and July of 1992. Now, excepting for purposes of our argument that Mr. Mucic admitted and took command of the camp at the end of July 1992, how can he be held responsible for what happened in May, June, and July? The Trial Chamber does agree, in paragraph 745 of the judgement, that the Prosecution has the burden of proving that Mr. Mucic was the commander of Celebici prison camp and that the standard of proof in this respect is beyond a reasonable doubt. Moreover, while downplaying the actual date upon which Mr. Mucic became a commander as being unnecessary in the discharge of the Prosecution's burden of proof, it framed the issue, in paragraph 745, as whether he was the commander during the relevant period as set forth in the indictment. We think that's very important. The Trial Chamber boasted that there was "a plethora" of evidence brought forth by the Prosecution on the issue, backdating, so to speak, the de facto authority in May of 1992. And it's our submission that a reliance on that evidence is unreasonable and an evaluation of that evidence is appropriate. I'd like the Trial Chamber to note that some of the testimony relied upon by the Trial Chamber, and I will go over some of it in detail, is inherently unreasonable. The Trial Chamber cites the evidence of several witnesses that give "evidence of the actual exercise of authority over Celebici prison camp by Mucic," and that's starting in paragraph 745 of the judgement. The Trial Chamber states that Witness P stated that Mr. Mucic transferred him in June 1992 from Celebici. When one looks at the citation at page 4518 of the transcript, the transcript reveals that Witness P was never transferred from Celebici in June 1992. Witness P also never said that Mr. Mucic was a commander. Witness P only said that Mr. Mucic said he was being forced to take over the camp sometime in the future. That's at 4519 of the transcript. Why is that important? Because the Trial Chamber cites Witness P as stating that Mucic transferred him in June 1992, when in fact that didn't happen. That's an example of the Trial Chamber's unreasonableness on the, "actual exercise of authority." At paragraph 746 of the judgement, Witness N claimed that Mr. Mucic was the commander because when "Pavo" was to come to the hangar, Mr. Delic would say the commander was coming. Now, if you look at the transcript citation there at pages 1923 to 1924, the question Witness N was asked was when did he see Mucic for the first time. And the answer was he didn't recall the exact date, but he remembered seeing him in August 1992. Now, I harp on this issue simply because, again, the backdating of the de facto command to May of 1992 is being substantiated by witnesses that are cited in the Trial Chamber's judgement. And we don't think that the evaluation of that evidence, when you look at it, was done in a reasonable fashion. Also at paragraph 746 of the judgement, Stevan Gligorevic, he was cited for giving testimony to similar effect as Witness N and Witness P. The question put to him relied upon by the Trial Chamber as "exercise of authority" was: Did you see Mr. Mucic in camp? And on page 1453 of the transcript, the answer was, "I saw him, but I cannot determine the exact time. I think it was the end of June/early July," and this is in 1992. But then the following question, or the previous question, which is I think is critical, is on 1451 and 1452 of the transcript. Question: "Did you see any of these now-named persons exercising command in the camp?" And by "any of these now-named persons," he was referring to Delic or Delalic or Mucic. And the answer was: "Yes, I saw Delic, because we all had to obey him, because all the guards had to obey him and they were even afraid of him. I don't know about Pavo Mucic. I cannot recall when I saw him for the first time. I cannot remember exactly, but I think it was somewhere late June or early July." So when you look at some of the citations in the Trial Chamber's judgement to what evidence is that shows "effective control," when you look at the evidence, it doesn't show anything. Interestingly, he was asked on the same page of the transcript, that is, this particular witness, Mr. Gligorevic, if and in what way you saw Delic exercising command. The answer was: "That was obvious. There was no question there. At least at that time what was obvious is there was reasonable doubt on behalf of Mr. Gligorevic's impressions of Mucic as a commander. Paragraph 746 of the judgement also cites Vaso Dordic. On page 4348 of the transcript, the Trial Chamber relies upon Dordic's testimony that Mucic identified himself as the commander on July 13th. He did not see Mucic but for one occasion ten days later. And under cross-examination, Mr. Dordic pointed out that he never mentioned July 13th in some other statements that he gave to the OTP. In paragraph 747 of the judgement, Mirko Dordic, on page 4796 of the transcript, said he saw him in camp once in June. The next time was the end of July/beginning of August 1992. Similarly, Mr. Branko Sudar, in transcript page 5751. The only thing mentioned here is that Sudar claims when Pavo Mucic's name was mentioned, the guard stopped beating detainees. And then what's I think interesting about that quotation is that he says, "In the meantime, they said half of us should get ready to go to Musala, Konjic, half of them left, then I stayed behind. Then when the van came a second time, the rest of us got in and we were driven to the sports hall in Konjic, known as Musala." Nothing here mentions Mr. Mucic's name or in any way associates him with the transfer or that Mr. Mucic was ever even seen. The Trial Chamber also in the judgement makes a big deal about an exhibit, number 192, in an article from an Arab newspaper which was shown to be copied to the camp. Based upon the discussions at transcript 8476 to 8515, the Trial Chamber at that point didn't put much validity into that. In fact, Judge Jan stated, "It has appeared in the press, nothing more than that." In our view, to cite that as authority for Mucic as a commander is completely unreasonable. The article itself gave no indication of reliability for issues pertaining to command authority or command responsibility. Mr. Nedeljko Draganic, another witness relied upon by the Trial Chamber in the judgement for vestiges of command, in paragraph 756 stated in the transcript that Mr. Mucic released him on 30 August of 1992 and that he didn't recall when he first saw Mucic but saw him one or two times. During his entire stay he is quoted as saying, on pages 1612 and 1613, of the transcript, "I didn't know who had authority," and he was there for 90 days. Dragan Kuljanin, there was no testimony with respect to timing of command. Mladin Kuljanin, in a transcript and cited in the judgement, says he saw Mr. Mucic a couple of times in the camp in September, and he was interviewed in June in the camp, in the command building, by two people, neither of whom were Mucic. Paragraph 758 of the judgement has several witnesses: Novica Dordic, Witness B, Zoran Ninkovic, none of whom identified Mr. Mucic as the commander, or had no idea who he was in terms of command. Interestingly, Mr. Ninkovic, who said he saw Mr. Mucic in Celebici for the first and last time on June 6th, said in his transcript, "The first commander who introduced himself was Rale Musinovic." That's testimony on 51, 52, and at 51, 53 of the trial transcript. What I'm driving at here, at least for the sake of argument, is the only reasonable, credible evidence of Mr. Mucic in command begins late July, early August of 1992. Now, we don't have a quarrel with the Trial Chamber making the statement that Mr. Mucic was in Celebici, present there before the end of May 1992. I think that's pretty clear. However, using that presence, the Trial Chamber, in our estimation, leaps to the conclusion that not only was he present but he was exercising de facto authority over the prison camp and its personnel, and we believe, given some of the testimony that I pointed out in oral argument thus far, that that's unreasonable. It's also unreasonable with respect to control in May, June, and July of 1992, to cite documents in paragraph 764 of the document, Exhibit 75, 84, 91, and 158. These are all documents signed at the end of August. How this implies de facto control in May, June, and July, to us, is beyond comprehension. Interestingly, after a very important witness testified on behalf of Mr. Delalic, his name was Sadik Dzumhur, who was in the camp as a MUP commander in May and June of 1992, after everyone got done questioning him, Judge Karibi-Whyte, on 2305 to 2306 asked him a series of questions about who -- "Do you know who the person was in charge of the prisons at Celebici? Who was the head at that time, up until June 15th of 1992 at least?" And Dzumhur answered: "Up until June 15th, I know that a MUP unit was accommodated in Celebici and that heading that unit was Rale Musinovic." Then Judge Karibi-Whyte further followed up: "And you know that the MUP was in charge of the prisoners, they were looking after the persons detained there?" And the answer is: "In that period, yes." The further follow-up question the Judge asked: "When did they cease to take charge of the persons in the prison there?" Answer: "I don't know exactly, but I said about mid-June new TO forces arrived and several policemen remained behind." Now, I don't think there is any question that Mr. Mucic was not a member of MUP. We don't believe that there's reasonable, credible testimony putting him commander in May and June and most of July of 1992, and ignoring Mr. Dzumhur's evidence and testimony makes the conclusion that he was the commander at that time frame de facto unreasonable. While there is evidence of Mr. Mucic being in camp before the end of July, such presence, in our humble opinion, does not prove or indicate beyond a reasonable doubt that he was at that given moment the commander or the administrator of the camp. As you will have surmised by reading the judgement and by reading most of the documentation in this case, entry into the camp by those who had no function there was very easy to achieve. The question that I put on the de jure or the de facto control is where is the actual responsibility or the actual evidence of superior authority in May, June, and July of 1992? That's why we urge, in reviewing the judgement, that close looks are taken at some of the citations that the Trial Chamber has used in the record to "prove control" at the relevant time frames in May to November of 1992, and we believe that no reasonable, credible evidence exists to show that control existed at least in May, June, and July of 1992. Thank you very much Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, very few submissions I wish to make partly, because most have been made by my learned friend Mr. Moran, although matters have been raised by the Prosecution with which we take no issue, and also because it is suspected that the documents that we hope will become apparent may answer some of the questions in the affirmative that we seek affirmative answers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Before you go on, we don't want to forget that the status of your appeal or at least how long it should be pending for, and before we finish with you, we better be ready to sort that one out. I don't want you to do it now, I just want to remind you that we haven't dealt with it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: To some extent I very much appreciate that I'm being asked to calculate the length of a piece of string at the moment, because we haven't actually got the documents that may determine -- did I misunderstand Your Honour? The whole length of the appeal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think you can take it that we will grant you the same as we have granted the Prosecution, that your appeal may be left open, but we have not yet considered the basis upon which or the length of time which you should have. I don't want you to estimate times, but the Prosecution are being required, in effect, to make their application without a full understanding of the documents, and you should be in a different position because you are looking for everything there that will assist you to meet a case. Now, that's all I mean. We have to deal with that at some stage before we have finished with your ground of appeal 9, as it now is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will certainly put our minds to that matter and give as reasonable an explanation as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We will deal with it obviously in the morning, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm much obliged for that. There's very little in my submission that bears repetition in this life except perhaps feeding children and constitutional monarchy, but one question that I would pose, a submission I would pose, and that is I appreciate by doing this I'm actually asking the Appeals Chamber to consider this matter rather than supply an answer to it through submission, and that's this: As an Appellate Chamber, you are, of course, lawmakers. The law relating to de jure/de facto command responsibility is far from certain. As my learned friend Mr. Moran said, he's not even entirely sure what de facto command responsibility is because of the lack of real definition. What I ask the Appeals Chamber to bear in mind is simply this: That there must be species of executive authority that are exercised by people who have the ability, in the heat of the moment, or in the circumstances in which they find themselves, to exercise such authority without it being in the camp of either de facto or de jure command responsibility, because otherwise, if every act of executive power, however minor it was, was determined to fall into one or other camp, there would be no delimitation on command responsibility and we would be getting away from the essence of command, and we would fall to a situation where everybody who exercised any authority or initiative at all was at risk of that exercise being cloaked with the mantle of command responsibility, and in the context of these matters, criminal command responsibility, because it seems -- its self-evident that the whole doctrine of command responsibility in international law is to give rise to judicial sanction in respect of criminal behaviour rather than what might be called beneficial or humanitarian acts, and that is a distinction which I would invite the Appellate Chamber to draw when considering this matter. Those -- it is self-evident, in my submission, whether any given act would broadly fall into the category of benevolent or malevolent and there is evidence in this case that Pavo Mucic did a number of acts which could only be described as benevolent, and I will come on to those later in the sentencing submissions. But I ask that the Appellate Chamber gives thought during the course of its determinations in that case to that aspect, because it seems to me that that's an area of law which needs to be addressed. Unless Your Honour has any questions, I do not intend to repeat anything that my learned friends have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. Now, Mr. Ackerman, you have to respond to the Prosecution grounds 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I begin -- this is horribly loud. I begin in a bit of a quandary similar to that one I was in this morning when the Prosecution began to argue a matter which I did not think had been scheduled for argument. One of the things that's on my plate to argue is the issue of Count 48 and the Prosecutor's contention that -- Prosecutor's contention that Mr. Delalic should have been convicted under Count 48 because of his status as an aider and abettor. The Prosecution, unless the fast talk was going so fast that I missed it, did not argue that issue. It's point 3, I believe. Now, whether they intend then to abandon that or not, I don't know, but I'm not real comfortable responding to an argument that was not made, and I don't know whether Mr. Farrell now wants to address that or wants to announce to the Court that he's abandoned it or what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He is relying upon his written submissions as expanded in Court. If he hasn't expanded upon it, that does not mean he's withdrawn the written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's fine. The only thing I'm pointing out is that was never said. If he's relying on his written submissions, that's fine with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think I made it sufficiently clear at the various pre-appeal conferences we don't want counsel reading out what they have already put in writing, but we are taking into account what has been put in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now clear to me. Along that line, Your Honour, I took it very seriously when you announced at the Status Conference that we should not stand up here and tell you what we have written in our briefs, and I've taken that seriously, and I suspect that you will consider very carefully the things that I have written in my brief regarding these various issues. Now, I have noticed, sitting here today, that some of the parties have, nonetheless, taken the opportunity to spend some time telling you what it is they've written in their briefs. I will not do that. What I will do is tell you the things that I believe have occurred since the brief was filed that might be of interest to you regarding the various issues. I want to begin by discussing the question of the definition of "knew or had reason to know." The Prosecution is correct. The real issue here is the definition of "had reason to know." Candidly, the Prosecution has admitted what I contended in my brief, that this was really an academic exercise because it didn't play any role whatsoever in the decision the Trial Chamber arrived at with regard to Mr. Delalic. I will point out, however, in the nature of that academic exercise, that since the Celebici decision, the Aleksovski Trial Chamber has considered the definition of the phrase "knew or had reason to know" and adopted the Celebici Trial Chamber definition at page 80 of their decision. So by that point, six Judges had agreed with the definition that was set out in the Celebici Trial Chamber's decision. I think it's significant that in the Aleksovski appeal, the Office of the Prosecutor chose not to challenge the Aleksovski Trial Chamber's adoption of the Celebici Trial Chamber's definition of that phrase. The Aleksovski Trial Chamber did speak, and this gets into a number of issues that we're discussing, and that is the kind of circumstantial evidence that one might consider in terms of determining whether someone may have had reason to know. I won't go into that in any detail except to say that that is set out both in Celebici and in Aleksovski, the Trial Chamber decisions. In the Blaskic case, the Trial Chamber fashioned a somewhat different definition of "had reason to know." In Blaskic, they talked about ignorance not being a defence if the absence of knowledge is the result of negligence in the discharge of his duties. That's at paragraph 332. Again, this has no real effect on the Delalic case since he had no duty to know, according to the Trial Chamber, what was going on in Celebici because there was no superior/subordinate relationship there, so he couldn't have negligently discharged any duty by failing to acquire that knowledge. I think that's all I had to say with regard to that issue that has come up basically since the Trial Chamber's decision. If I may, unless there's no question about that issue, I will move on to this issue of superior responsibility. I've heard a number of things sitting here this morning that I think I first want to discuss. Mr. Moran, I believe, was asked the question about the inherent power of a commander. If you are a commander, do you have the inherent power to punish? And the answer was yes, that can be taken without proof. However, if there is proof to the contrary, then that must be considered, which was the case in the Celebici case with respect to Mr. Delalic's role as commander of TG-1. A number of military people came here and testified, Polutak is one that comes to mind, that in the case of a tactical group, a tactical group is made up of regular units that are detached from their normal structure and made part of a tactical group to accomplish a particular purpose and then returned back to their original units. The experts that testified about that said the tactical group commander does not have the power to punish violations committed by members of his tactical group, that his only power is to refer those to the commander of the group that is attached to his unit for the tactical purpose, whatever it is. So that would be a case where although the power is inherent, there is evidence to the contrary, that there is no such power. Mr. Farrell talked at some length about bits of evidence that you can find in the record which tend to show that Mr. Delalic exercised some authority over the alleged perpetrators of the crimes at Celebici, and clearly the Trial Chamber was aware of those bits of evidence. It would be surprising if they had indicted Mr. Delalic and tried him if they had not had some evidence that would tend to indicate that he might have had that kind of relationship with Celebici. What we didn't hear from Mr. Farrell and what is the most important thing is that the Prosecution's burden was not to show just some evidence but to prove that beyond a reasonable doubt. Now, if you look at the full body of evidence from the Celebici case, about the role of Mr. Delalic in 1992 in the Konjic area, the evidence is almost overwhelming that he did not exercise any control or command over Celebici. The Trial Chamber found that there was no superior/subordinate relationship between Mr. Delalic and the people who operated that camp, and they found that based upon looking at all the evidence. They say at the beginning of their opinion that they've considered all the evidence and that the Prosecution had failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that there was this superior/subordinate relationship. A thing that has concerned me since reading the Prosecution's brief, and it has come up again today, is the Prosecution keeps referring to evidence not rejected by the Trial Chamber. They'll say to you, "Your Honours, there was this exhibit or there was this testimony, and it was not rejected by the Trial Chamber, so you must take it into consideration." There is no rule at this Tribunal that when a Trial Chamber writes its judgement it must single out each of those pieces of evidence that it found to be not credible, that it rejected. What you can best do, from looking at the judgement that the Celebici Trial Chamber wrote, is understand that some evidence was credited more than other evidence was, and just because there is testimony for a particular proposition, and what comes to mind is the testimony that Mr. Farrell was talking about with regard to Dr. Grubac and his release from prison, just because people said that "Mr. Delalic said he would release me," doesn't mean that the Trial Chamber gave that any credit whatsoever. And just because the Trial Chamber didn't say, "We reject this evidence," that you must then give it credit. I think it's clear from the decision of the Trial Chamber that a lot of evidence of that nature was not credited by them. And they were the ones who sat, Your Honours, where you are sitting now and looked the witnesses in the eye when they testified, saw their demeanour when they testified, saw the way they said the things they said, saw whether they kind of held their hand over their face and looked away when they said certain things. Only the judge who is in a position to make that credibility determination can decide whether or not that evidence should be accepted or not. Looking at the cold record of the trial, reading the transcript off the television or off a cold transcript, all you see are the words. You don't see the tone of voice, you don't see the shifty eye, you don't see the things that we all use when we communicate with others to make a determination as to whether or not we're being told the truth. You have to give credit to those people who sat where you are in Celebici for having made that determination correctly and properly. There is this issue -- frankly, when I first saw it in the Prosecution's brief, it almost took my breath away -- the proposition that in the context of command responsibility there should be a component that says: If you are a person of influence, even though not within the superior/subordinate relationship, but a person of influence, that there are circumstances under which you could be held responsible as if you were a superior in that relationship. The Prosecution, in my mind, is asking you to make new law, asking you to adopt a whole new theory of command responsibility. When other people have talked to you today, others of my colleagues have talked to you today about that, there has been some talk about the uncertainty of trying to get our hands around that issue. Mr. Fenrick talked about it, how it was difficult to define, and he was only able to give you a couple of examples of what it is not: It is not this and it's not this. But he wasn't able to give you any examples of what it is. One of the things the rule of law requires is that if you're going to make some kind of behaviour subject to a criminal sanction, that you must define it in such a way that reasonable people will be able to understand what it is they're being asked to either do or not do. When this Tribunal is being asked to adopt a principle that no one can stand up here and define for you so that you can understand it, how on earth can those out there in the field who are expected to comply with it understand what it is they are to do and not do? Take Konjic and that situation that went on there in 1992. Every village of that size, we all know from our own experience, may have any number of people who are influential. The mayor of the town may be a particularly popular doctor in the town. Certainly the president of the War Presidency in Konjic would have been an influential person. Any number of people there have influence. The Prosecutor is saying if you knew and had any kind of influence over the person who was in charge of the camp, who was responsible for Celebici, then it was your duty to take some kind of steps to stop what was happening there. And my submission is that that is -- first of all, it is not part of customary international law, and this Court can only apply what is customary international law. And you have to determine, if you're going to apply customary international law, that it is beyond doubt part of customary international law. And there is no way, looking at all of the history of the concept of command responsibility, that you could ever arrive at the conclusion that it is beyond doubt part of customary international law that a person of influence in the community can be held responsible as a commander or as a superior even though he's not within the superior/subordinate relationship. The Trial Chamber found, and the Prosecutor agreed in their brief, that Mr. Delalic was not within the superior/subordinate relationship as regards Celebici. So the only way that he can be held responsible, and that's why the Prosecutor suggests this new approach, is to be held responsible as a person of influence who's outside that superior/subordinate relationship and can somehow have the power to effect it. The Celebici Trial Chamber's view of the law regarding command responsibility has been largely adopted by subsequent decisions and judgements in this Tribunal. The Blaskic trial adopted the Celebici definition at paragraph 300 and 301 of their decision, the Trial Chamber. Aleksovski appeals judgement in essence agreed with the Celebici definition. One of the things that runs throughout these is element 1, is the existence of a superior/subordinate relationship. That's element 1 of defining whether or not someone can be held responsible. That decision, by the way, by the Aleksovski Trial Chamber again was not appealed by the OTP. They did not challenge the Aleksovski Trial Chamber's agreement with the Celebici definition of command responsibility. The Aleksovski Appeals Chamber said that this relationship, superior/subordinate, can be determined by asking whether the accused had the ability to give orders and punish the persons involved. And clearly the Trial Chamber in Celebici found that Delalic did not have that ability, based upon all the evidence that they considered. We've argued in our brief about the approach taken by the drafters of the Rome Statute in this regard. The Rome Statute reads: "A superior shall be criminally responsible for crimes within the jurisdiction of the Court committed by subordinates under his or her effective authority and control." I must grant to Mr. Fenrick, even though there have been times when he didn't think they were important, that there are some cases that go somewhat beyond that that came out of the post-World War II period. I think it's a safe conclusion that the thinking in those cases has basically been rejected since World War II by the world community. You have the most recent evidence of the world community adopting the Rome Statute, and I suggest to you that that language in the Rome Statute is the world community's current view of what customary international law at that time was, which they then codified in that Statute. Prior to that you have the earlier work, post-World War II work, of the international law commission, which arrived at roughly the same position regarding this definition in this regard. I suggest to you that it would be both poor policy and a violation of your mandate from the United Nations to now adopt some new approach to this which is not consistent with either the International Law Commission's view or the Rome Statute. I think it would violate the principle of nullem crimen sine lege and that it would be improper for this Tribunal to establish a test and a rule regarding command responsibility for the people appearing before this Tribunal that will not be imposed by the International Criminal Court upon people appearing before that court when it finally begins to function. Finally, I want to point out that in the Celebici trial, on this issue of what Mr. Delalic's position was in the Konjic area during 1992, Mr. Delalic had a number of witnesses that the Trial Chamber did not permit him to call regarding that. The Trial Chamber shut down the Delalic defence and prevented him from bringing before the Chamber a number of witnesses regarding this issue. It seems to me in that context, where the Trial Chamber decided that they had heard enough evidence about Mr. Delalic's lack of responsibility for what occurred within Celebici and didn't want to hear anymore, that it would be decidedly improper to now reverse that judgement and find Mr. Delalic guilty, having been prevented from fully defending himself at the Trial Chamber level. I'm completed with my argument regarding that issue. I don't know how long you want to go. I'm prepared to do everything that I've been asked to talk about at this point if the Chamber wants to sit here and have me do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean in relation to the Prosecution's appeal, or are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In relation to the issues that are on my plate right now. I think there are two more that I have to discuss: the rebuttal/reopen issue and the unlawful confinement issue. And I think I can finish those, Your Honour, in 10 or 15 minutes, or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it would be preferable if we came back to it tomorrow, Mr. Ackerman, and we'll start with you in the morning. Then the Prosecution will have the right to respond to Mr. Mucic's appeal and to reply to everybody. As there are three of you, I hope you've sorted it out between yourselves on the Prosecution side who is going to deal with what and that there will not be any repetition. We'll adjourn now until 10 tomorrow.
